title: Austrian State Treasury Note for Five Thousand Crowns
description: A Viennese bearer treasury note issued by the Austrian state in 1920 for 5,000 Kronen, this note is designated as tax-free and interest-bearing, with provisions for redemption by the state debt administration. The note's design reveals how the visual language of Art Nouveau had permeated the visual culture of the Viennese state. Issued in the immediate aftermath of World War I and the dissolution of the Habsburg Empire, this bond represents the new Austrian republic's efforts to raise capital during a period of severe economic instability and hyperinflation. This is further in conversation with the values of opulence, wealth, and extravagance espoused by the aesthetic values of Art Nouveau rippling throughout Europe at the time.
creator: Republic of Austria, Österreichische Staatsschuldenverwaltung
notes: Austrian State Treasury Note, Serie 1920b, No. 008,255, 5,000 Kronen, tax-free. Vienna, September 1, 1920. Signed by the Staatsschuldenverwaltung.
transcription:
# Austrian State Treasury Note for Five Thousand Kronen — Transcription

## Original (German):

**(top center: Austrian double-headed eagle coat of arms)**

**Serie 1920b     5000 K     № 008,255**

Steuerfreier 6%iger, 6jähriger, jederzeit ¼jährlich kündbarer

**Österreichischer Staatsschatzschein
über Fünftausend Kronen**

Die Staatszentralkassa in Wien zahlt an den Inhaber dieses auf Grund des Gesetzes vom 22. Juli 1920, St. G. Bl. Nr. 330, ausgegebenen Schatzscheines an dem durch die Kündigung bestimmten Tage, spätestens am 1. September 1926, den Betrag von 5000 Kronen. Der Inhaber ist berechtigt, diesen Schatzschein jederzeit für den ersten Tag des der Kündigung nachfolgenden vierten Kalendermonates zur Rückzahlung zum Nennwert zu kündigen. Die Kündigung erfolgt unter Vorbehalt des Schatzscheines im Inland bei der Staatszentralkassa, bei der Öster.-ungar. Bank, Hauptanstalt Wien und ihren Filialen in Österreich sowie bei dem Postsparkassenamt Wien und bei den Postämtern, im Auslande bei den bekanntgegebenen Zahlstellen. Hiebei wird die erfolgte Kündigung auf dem Schatzscheine ersichtlich gemacht. Dieser Schatzschein wird mit sechs Prozent für das Jahr verzinst. Die Zinsen werden ohne Abzug einer Rentensteuer halbjährlich im nachhinein am 1. März und 1. September eines jeden Jahres an den Inhaber der zu diesem Schatzscheine gehörigen Zinsscheine bei der Staatszentralkassa in Wien ausgezahlt. Die Verzinsung erlischt mit dem Fälligkeitstage des Kapitalbetrages. Der Schatzschein ist zwecks Einlösung samt den bis zum Fälligkeitstage noch nicht fällig gewordenen Zinsscheinen zurückzustellen; die bis zum Fälligkeitstage entfallenden Stückzinsen werden gegen Einziehung des laufenden Zinsscheines vergütet, der Betrag der fehlenden noch nicht fälligen Zinsscheine vom Kapitalbetrage in Abzug gebracht. Die Rückzahlung des Kapitals erfolgt ohne Steuer, Gebühren oder sonstige Abzüge bei der Staatszentralkassa in Wien. Der Anspruch aus dem Schatzscheine erlischt durch Verjährung in Ansehung der Zinsen binnen sechs Jahren, in Ansehung des Kapitals binnen 30 Jahren vom Fälligkeitstage an. Dieser Schatzschein ist mit 12 Zinsscheinen, von denen der erste am 1. März 1921 fällig wird, versehen.

Wien, am 1. September 1920.

Der Staatssekretär für Finanzen [signature]

Dieser Schatzschein ist gesetzmäßig begeben und im Hauptbuch der Staatsschuld eingetragen.

Der Präsident des Staatsrechnungshofes: [signature]

**(bottom, blank fill-in form for redemption)**

Zur Rückzahlung für den 1. ..................... 192.... gekündigt.

........................ am .......................... 192....

---

## English Translation:

**(top center: Austrian double-headed eagle coat of arms)**

**Series 1920b     5000 K     № 008,255**

Tax-free, 6%, six-year, cancellable at any time on a quarterly basis

**Austrian State Treasury Note
for Five Thousand Kronen**

The Central State Treasury in Vienna pays to the bearer of this treasury note — issued on the basis of the law of 22 July 1920, State Law Gazette No. 330 — on the day determined by the notice of redemption, at the latest on 1 September 1926, the amount of 5000 Kronen. The bearer is entitled to give notice of redemption of this treasury note at any time, at face value, effective as of the first day of the fourth calendar month following the notice. Notice of redemption is given, with the treasury note being surrendered, within the country at the Central State Treasury, at the Austro-Hungarian Bank, Head Institution Vienna, and its branches in Austria, as well as at the Postal Savings Bank Office Vienna and at the post offices; abroad, at the publicly announced paying agencies. The notice of redemption given is thereupon noted on the treasury note. This treasury note bears interest at six percent per year. The interest is paid, without deduction of any annuity tax, semi-annually in arrears on 1 March and 1 September of each year to the bearer of the interest coupons belonging to this treasury note, at the Central State Treasury in Vienna. Interest ceases on the maturity date of the principal amount. For redemption, the treasury note must be surrendered together with the interest coupons not yet fallen due up to the maturity date; the accrued interest falling due up to the maturity date is reimbursed against surrender of the current interest coupon, and the amount of the missing, not-yet-due interest coupons is deducted from the principal amount. Repayment of the principal is made without tax, fees, or other deductions at the Central State Treasury in Vienna. The claim under the treasury note lapses by prescription with respect to interest after six years, and with respect to the principal after 30 years from the maturity date. This treasury note is provided with 12 interest coupons, the first of which falls due on 1 March 1921.

Vienna, 1 September 1920.

The State Secretary for Finance [signature]

This treasury note has been lawfully issued and entered in the ledger of the state debt.

The President of the State Audit Office: [signature]

**(bottom, blank fill-in form for redemption)**

Called for repayment on the 1st ..................... 192.... .

........................ on .......................... 192....

title: Burmese Government Bond
description: This is a rare surviving example of financial documentation from wartime Burma, notable for its exclusive use of the indigenous script at a politically turbulent moment in Burmese history. A Burmese government bond written in native Burmese script, denominated Ten Kyat. The note's design speaks to the juxtaposition of Burmese script with European visual motifs, and the assertion of a uniquely post-colonial Burmese identity. Beneath the central vignette runs the national slogan, "One Blood, One Voice, One Command," the rallying motto of Ba Maw's wartime State of Burma. The footer carries a date in the Burmese calendar — year 1305 (1943/44 CE) — when Burma operated as a nominally independent state under Japanese occupation, following decades of British colonial rule.
creator: Government of Burma
notes: Approximate date ca. 1943-1945 based on historical context of Japanese-occupied Burma

**State of Burma Independence Savings Bond** (*Bama Naingngandaw Lut-lat-yay Ngwe-su Sachouk*)

**Ten Kyat** (*ta-hsè kyat*)

Series letter: **ka** (က) — printed in red on both sides of the centre.

title: Internal State Loan for National Defense
description: A Bulgarian government bearer bond for the 5% Internal State Loan of 1941, raised "for the National Defense" — 5,000 leva at 5% interest, issued through the Main Directorate of State and State-Guaranteed Debts. By 1941 Tsar Boris III's government had aligned Bulgaria with the Axis and needed to pay for mobilization, but sharply higher taxes risked resentment at home and heavy foreign borrowing would have strained the currency. Selling patriotic national-defense bonds to Bulgarians offered a third path: the state raised capital from its own citizens and promised repayment with interest rather than simply taxing them — turning private savings into war finance, and the people funding the war into its creditors.
creator: Kingdom of Bulgaria, Main Directorate of State Debts
notes: Approximate issue date; exact date not visible on document
transcription:
# Bulgarian 5% Internal State Loan of 1941 for the National Defence — Bearer Bond — Transcription

## Original (Bulgarian):

*(Ornate engraved border with fan rosettes at the corners; text is centred within the frame.)*

**ЦАРСТВО БЪЛГАРИЯ**
*(royal coat of arms — crowned lion shield — centred between the two words)*

**ГЛАВНА ДИРЕКЦИЯ НА ДЪРЖАВНИТѢ И НА ГАРАНТИРАНИТѢ
ОТЪ ДЪРЖАВАТА ДЛЪГОВЕ**

**5% ВЪТРЕШЕНЪ ДЪРЖАВЕНЪ ЗАЕМЪ отъ 1941 г.**
**ЗА НАРОДНАТА ОТБРАНА**

*(fine print, small type:)*

Издаденъ възъ основа на закона за 5% вътрешенъ държавенъ заемъ за нуждитѣ на народната отбрана, утвърденъ съ указъ № 3 отъ 24 май 1941 година, обнародванъ въ Държавенъ вестникъ, брой 116 отъ 30 май 1941 година и на законитѣ за измѣнението и допълнението му, утвърдени съ указъ № 4 отъ 15 юлий 1941 год. и № 1 отъ 26 януарий 1942 год., обнародвани въ Държавенъ вестникъ, брой 155 отъ 18 юлий 1941 год. и брой 20 отъ 29 януарий 1942 год.

*(central decorative panel:)*

**ОБЛИГАЦИЯ**
ОТЪ ПЕТЬ ХИЛЯДИ ЛЕВА
**5000    ЛЕВА    5000**
**5%**

Серия Б          № 022882
**НА ПРИНОСИТЕЛЯ**

*(main body text:)*

Заемътъ се представлява отъ облигации въ отрѣзки отъ 1.000, 5.000, 20.000, 50.000, 100.000, 500.000 и 1.000.000 лева.

Облигациитѣ носятъ 5% годишна лихва, платима въ края на всѣко шестмесечие, срещу купони съ падежъ 15 януарий и 15 юлий всѣка година.

Падежътъ на първия купонъ е 15 юлий 1942 година.

Погасяването на облигациитѣ ще се извършва шестмесечно въ срокъ отъ 15 години, на 15 януарий и 15 юлий всѣка година, чрезъ шестмесечни тегления по жребие.

Тегленията ще се извършватъ въ Главната дирекция на държавнитѣ и на гарантиранитѣ отъ държавата длъгове, единъ месецъ преди настъпване падежътъ на всѣки купонъ.

Първото теглене ще стане на 15 юлий 1942 година.

Купонитѣ съ изтекълъ падежъ и изтеглените въ погашение облигации се изплащатъ отъ Българската народна банка. Изплащането на изтеглените въ погашение облигации става едновременно съ купона, падежътъ на който настъпва следъ тегленето.

Представенитѣ за изплащане облигации трѣбва да бѫдатъ придружени съ всички купони, падежътъ на които не е настъпилъ на опредѣлената за плащане дата; стойностьта на непредставените купони се спада отъ капитала, който следва да се изплати на приносителя.

Непредставенитѣ за изплащане купони, за продължение на 5 години отъ деня на падежа имъ, се погасяватъ въ ползата на държавното съкровище. Този срокъ за погасенитѣ облигации е 15 години.

София, 15 декемврий 1941 година

*(signature block, three legends with handwritten signatures below:)*

ГЛАВЕНЪ ДИРЕКТОРЪ НА ДЪРЖАВНИТѢ ДЛЪГОВЕ:            МИНИСТЪРЪ НА ФИНАНСИТѢ:
*(handwritten signature)*                                              *(handwritten signature)*
ЗА КОНТРОЛЪ:
*(handwritten signature — [illegible])*

---

## English Translation:

*(Ornate engraved border with fan rosettes at the corners; text centred within the frame.)*

**KINGDOM OF BULGARIA** (Tsarstvo Bŭlgariya)
*(royal coat of arms — crowned lion shield — centred between the two words)*

**MAIN DIRECTORATE OF THE STATE AND STATE-GUARANTEED DEBTS**
(Glavna Direktsiya na Dŭrzhavnitě i na Garantiranitě otŭ Dŭrzhavata Dlŭgove)

**5% INTERNAL STATE LOAN of 1941**
**FOR THE NATIONAL DEFENCE** (Za Narodnata Otbrana)

*(fine print:)*

Issued on the basis of the law on the 5% Internal State Loan for the needs of the national defence, ratified by Decree No. 3 of 24 May 1941, promulgated in the State Gazette (Dŭrzhaven Vestnik), issue No. 116 of 30 May 1941, and of the laws for its amendment and supplement, ratified by Decree No. 4 of 15 July 1941 and No. 1 of 26 January 1942, promulgated in the State Gazette, issue No. 155 of 18 July 1941 and issue No. 20 of 29 January 1942.

*(central panel:)*

**BOND**
OF FIVE THOUSAND LEVA
**5000    LEVA    5000**
**5%**

Series Б (B)          No. 022882
**TO THE BEARER**

*(main body text:)*

The loan is represented by bonds in denominations of 1,000, 5,000, 20,000, 50,000, 100,000, 500,000 and 1,000,000 leva.

The bonds bear 5% annual interest, payable at the end of each half-year, against coupons falling due on 15 January and 15 July of each year.

The maturity of the first coupon is 15 July 1942.

The redemption of the bonds shall be carried out half-yearly over a term of 15 years, on 15 January and 15 July of each year, by means of half-yearly drawings by lot.

The drawings shall be carried out at the Main Directorate of the State and State-Guaranteed Debts, one month before the maturity of each coupon falls due.

The first drawing shall take place on 15 July 1942.

Coupons whose maturity has passed and bonds drawn for redemption are paid by the Bulgarian National Bank. Payment of bonds drawn for redemption is made simultaneously with the coupon whose maturity falls due after the drawing.

Bonds presented for payment must be accompanied by all coupons whose maturity has not fallen due on the date fixed for payment; the value of the coupons not presented is deducted from the principal to be paid to the bearer.

Coupons not presented for payment are extinguished in favour of the State Treasury after a further 5 years from the day of their maturity. This term for redeemed bonds is 15 years.

Sofia, 15 December 1941

*(signature block:)*

CHIEF DIRECTOR OF THE STATE DEBTS:            MINISTER OF FINANCE:
*(handwritten signature)*                                 *(handwritten signature)*
FOR CONTROL:
*(handwritten signature — [illegible])*

title: Pasquin's Windkaart: Dutch Satirical Playing Cards on the 1720 Windhandel
description: A set of fifty-five satirical playing cards, Pasquin's Wind-Card, from the Dutch compilation Het Groote Tafereel der Dwaasheid ("The Great Mirror of Folly"). The cards mock the windhandel, the speculative "wind trade" in company shares that gripped the Dutch Republic in 1720, each pairing an engraved figure with a Dutch verse that caricatures the speculators and promoters of the bubble. The King of Spades, for instance, shows a periwigged gentleman holding a balance in which a spade and a sheet of paper outweigh a purse of gold, paper wealth made absurdly heavier than real coin. As an object of shared play, the deck shows that financial satire reached beyond the elite forms of pamphlet and essay, traveling through cheap everyday print and the sociable spaces of taverns, coffeehouses, and parlors, where people handled cards and traded opinions.

pages.description:
**Pasquin's Windkaart: King of Spades — Paper Outweighs Gold**

The "Heer van Schoppen" (King of Spades): a periwigged gentleman holds a balance in which a spade and a sheet of paper outweigh a bag of gold, beneath the verse "De schop, en 't blad papier in de eene schaal gelegen, / Kan, door de Graversshoop, een goud beurs overwegen" — through the "Graversshoop" (gravediggers, a mocking term for speculators) the worthless scrip outweighs real coin. The card ridicules how paper shares came to be prized absurdly above the gold in hand. Page 1 of 55.

**Pasquin's Windkaart: Queen of Spades — The Frenzy of Quincampoix Ended**

Queen of Spades ("Vrouw", spade pip upper right). A finely dressed woman rests one hand on a spade thrust into the soil while tossing away her playing cards. The Dutch verse — "Men zet de schop vry neêr, ons spelen is verbruid… De blinde razernij van Quinquampoix heeft uit" — declares the gambling spoiled and the blind frenzy of Quincampoix over. Quincampoix, the Paris street at the heart of John Law's Mississippi scheme, stands here for the whole 1720 speculation; laying down the spade signals its collapse. Page 2 of 55.

**Pasquin's Windkaart: Jack of Spades — Prince Frederik's March to Vianen**

Knegt (Jack) of Spades, with spade pip inset. A drummer beats his drum as papers fly from the pack on his back; share-fools straggle off in the distance. Inscribed "Prins Fredriks mars, naar Vianen." The verse beats "Prins Fredriks mars" to march "de Actiegekken" like "wind zoldaten" (wind-soldiers) to Vianen — the debtors' refuge town whose banality underscores the maniacal, misguided pursuit of speculative wealth. Satirises the 1720 share-trading mania and the bankrupts fleeing to Vianen. Page 3 of 55.

**Pasquin's Windkaart: King of Hearts — The Laurel King Undone**

King of Hearts (inset heart marked "Heer"). A periwigged gentleman in coat and tricorne stands holding a small windmill emblem, labelled "Lauwer Koning" (Laurel King); behind him figures dig and toil on a barren slope. The verse reads "'k Heb de Actiës eerst bedagt, maar een kwade Actiekans / Smyt al myn lof omver, en schent myn lauwer krans" — satirising the 1720 share-trading (Actie) speculation mania of the Bubble year. Page 4 of 55.

**Pasquin's Windkaart: Queen of Hearts — The Share-Kettle**

Queen of Hearts ("Vrouw"), heart pip top-right. An elegantly gowned woman holds an engraving of a distilling still labelled with shares ("De Actie ketel"). The verse claims the share-kettle distilled "dat het papier in Goud verkeerd" (turns paper into gold), and that the schemer "Stookt goud uit klad papier, en maakt 't Heel-Al vol zotten" — boils gold from scrap paper and fills the world with fools. The card mocks how the engineers of such schemes were often their only beneficiaries. Page 5 of 55.

**Pasquin's Windkaart: Jack of Hearts — The Rogue Pierced by Regret**

Knave (Jack) of Hearts, labelled "Knegt of Boef" (Knave or Rogue). A man in coat and breeches plunges a blade into a large heart on his chest — "Uit Wanhoop" (out of despair). The verse describes a roguish heart that, led by a "reeks van Actiestreken" (string of share-dealing tricks) to seek profit, is "nu van spijt doorsteken" (now pierced through with regret). The card shows a naive speculator lamenting his trust in promises of untold riches. Page 6 of 55.

**Pasquin's Windkaart: King of Diamonds — Sheltered from the South and West Winds**

King of Diamonds (two diamond pips, inset "Heer"). A periwigged gentleman in tricorn and long coat stands in a doorway, one hand outstretched. Motto: "Ik ben beschermd, Daar ieder kermd" (I am protected, where all lament). The verse has him sheltered from "de Zuid en West hun windgeblaas" — the South Sea and West India companies' wind-trade of 1720. He claims to be enriched and protected by the schemes he perpetuates, yet the surrounding South and West winds imply his shelter is as fickle and short-lived as the speculation itself. Page 7 of 55.

**Pasquin's Windkaart: Queen of Diamonds — The Bursting Glass Bubble**

Queen ("Vrouw") of Diamonds (red diamond pip, top right). A finely dressed woman blows through a long pipe into a glass-furnace, forming a fragile glass bubble. The Dutch verse — "Door sterk te blázen breekt het glas, / Net als 't met de Actie-bubbels was" — likens the bursting glass to the collapse of the share ("Actie") bubbles of 1720. The card draws an idiomatic lesson: blow too hard and the glass shatters, just as unrestrained speculation destroys itself. Page 8 of 55.

**Pasquin's Windkaart: Jack of Diamonds — Scrip Turned to Smoke**

Knave of Diamonds ("Knegt", diamond pip upper right). A pipe-smoking man lights a paper share certificate with a burning-glass under a blazing sun, the verse reading "'t Papier zo duur / Werd rook door 't vuur" (the paper so dear became smoke by the fire) and "Mijn Actiebrief verteerd… hij kan geen zon verdragen" — his share certificate is consumed, unable to endure the sun. In the period's satire daylight stands for truth and scrutiny: the scrip that dazzled in the frenzy cannot survive exposure to reality. Page 9 of 55.

**Pasquin's Windkaart: King of Clubs — The Ruined Director**

King ("Heer") of Clubs. A finely dressed company director clutches papers, an empty sheet slipping from one hand; a monkey beside a funnel-topped pedestal empties coin. Motto: "Eerst gelukkig, Nu dronkkig" (first fortunate, now drunken). The verse laments "'k Ben Directeur geweest… het geld droop door de zak" — money slipped through the bag, leaving nothing but trouble. Ruin, the card shows, spared no rank; it presents the director's drunken fall as retribution for his insincerity, mocked further by the funneling monkey. Page 10 of 55.

**Pasquin's Windkaart: Queen of Clubs — Icarus and Phaethon**

Queen of Clubs ("Vrouw", klaveren pip top right). An elegantly dressed woman holds flowers and a basket while below her a falling Icarus-like figure tumbles toward the sea. The verse links her ruined husband to mythic over-reachers: "Met Ikarus en Faëton verdwijnt mijn man zijn Actie zon" (with Icarus and Phaethon my husband's share-sun vanishes). Though his speculative sun has fallen from the sky, she keeps her courage "zo lang ik met de klavers speel" — so long as she plays with clubs. Page 11 of 55.

**Pasquin's Windkaart: Jack of Clubs — From Servant to Gentleman**

Jack of Clubs ("Knegt", klaveren pip top-right). A man in a fur coat stands amid broken shackles, ships behind, a discarded lord's coat and hat on a chair. Motto: "'t Geluk brengt my / Uit slaverny" (fortune lifts me out of servitude). The verse boasts "Mijn Actiestar heeft mij van knegt tot Heer gemaakt" — his lucky share raised him from servant to gentleman. The card stages the bubble's classic inversion: servants rise to gentlemen while many a gentleman is reduced to begging. Page 12 of 55.

**Pasquin's Windkaart: Ace of Spades — Scrip Swept into Lethe**

Ace of Spades (single spade pip, numbered "1"). A hatted street-sweeper shovels refuse beside a broom and wheelbarrow, scattered papers at his feet. The motto "Men maakt zig 't vulnis kwyt" (one gets rid of the filth) leads to "Weg met dit klad papier… in lethes poel te vegen" — away with this worthless scrip, swept into the pool of Lethe. The card treats the shares of 1720 as stinking rubbish, fit only to be swept into oblivion. Page 13 of 55.

**Pasquin's Windkaart: Two of Spades — Father Time's Reckoning**

Two of Spades (spade pip and numeral "2"). A winged, bearded old man — Father Time — holds a smoking brazier and an earthen urn against a barren landscape, beneath the motto "Van al de Compagnien" (of all the companies). The verse declares "Ik ben 't die 't al ondekt, en 't klad papier verbrand… en help den Koopman weer in stand" — he who exposes all, burns the worthless paper, and restores the merchant. Time embodies the reckoning after the crash, forcing merchants to face their folly. Page 14 of 55.

**Pasquin's Windkaart: Three of Spades — Three Companies Afloat on Wind**

Three of Spades (spade pip and "3"). Three richly dressed women holding distaffs ride aloft, balanced on a shovel against the clouds. The verse — "Zie hoe de Zuid, en West, en Missisippi zweven / Op eene schop, wijl zij van lugt en winden leven" — shows South Sea, West India and Mississippi floating on a single spade, for they live on nothing but air and wind. One of the deck's sharpest strokes: the three great speculative schemes of 1720 are sustained entirely by hot air. Page 15 of 55.

**Pasquin's Windkaart: Four of Spades — The South Sea Dog Howls**

Four of Spades (spade pip and numeral "4"). A standing gentleman dangles a small dog by a whip-leash while another dog tumbles on its back below. The verse mocks: "Hoe schreeuwd de Zuidze-dog zo schrikkelijk, daar mijn kat / Naauw maauwd" — how dreadfully the South Sea dog howls, while my cat scarcely mews. The card compares the bubble's victims: the South Sea speculators cry loudest because they have felt most of the whip. Page 16 of 55.

**Pasquin's Windkaart: Five of Spades — The Fifth City Crushes the Shares**

Five of Spades ("5" with spade pip). A man holds out a balance bearing the Amsterdam arms — a shield with three St. Andrew's crosses ("XXX") — while a trumpeting putto flies overhead. The verse "Zie hoe de vijfde stad van Holland, de Acties plet… Waarom een lauwerkrans mij werd op 't hoofd gezet" shows the city crushing the shares and crowned with laurel for it. The "fifth city of Holland" is honoured here for resisting the speculative mania. Page 17 of 55.

**Pasquin's Windkaart: Six of Spades — Money Kept, Honour Sunk**

Six of Spades (pip and "6"). A shabby, torn-coated speculator stands by a battered chest, brandishing papers. The top motto "Een sesje min of meer / Scheeld weing aan mij eer" (a sixpence more or less matters little to my honour) gives way to "Mijn rotte kist… 't Behouw het geld wel, maar mijne eer, die is verzonken" — the rotten chest keeps the money, but his honour has sunk. The card marks a speculator who kept his gains at the cost of his good name. Page 18 of 55.

**Pasquin's Windkaart: Seven of Spades — The Reckoning at Quincampoix**

Seven of Spades (pip and numeral "7"). A long-coated gentleman stands at a table strewn with coins, dealing them out. The label "Drie en vier / Betaald alhier" (three and four paid here) and the verse "Zie de een en twe, en vijf en zes gaan vrij… De drie en vier betaald in Quinquempoix 't gelag" turn the dealing into a throw of dice. Quincampoix, the Paris street of John Law's Mississippi bubble, is where certain numbers pay the reckoning — the promise of riches left to chance. Page 19 of 55.

**Pasquin's Windkaart: Eight of Spades — Diogenes' Lantern for the White Falcon**

Eight of Spades (pip "8", spade emblem). A finely dressed man holds a paper bearing a white falcon and, atop a tall stool, a lit lantern. The motto "Diogenes lantaarn heb ik bij dag van noden… 't Vong de agtings Witte Valk die and'ren is ontvloden" invokes Diogenes' lantern in broad daylight to seek the rare White Falcon of esteem that has fled the others. As Diogenes sought an honest man, the speaker hunts for something rare and vanished amid the bubble madness. Page 20 of 55.

**Pasquin's Windkaart: Nine of Spades — Folly, Prudence, and the Grave of Art**

Nine of Spades ("9" with spade pip). A fool in a nightcap holds a mirror and an unrolled print of a crowded scene, a digging spade beside him. The verse — "De dwaasheid dogt de kunst te delven in het graf, / Maar vrouw Voorzigtigheid keerd deze rampen af" — has Folly try to bury art in the grave while Lady Prudence wards off the disaster. The card sets the enduring worth of art and humanity against the flighty chaos of greed and speculation. Page 21 of 55.

**Pasquin's Windkaart: Ten of Spades — The Tomb of the Share-Prince**

Ten of Spades (pip and "10"). A ragged, tattered beggar in a broad hat stands in open country, holding up a coin and carrying an alms-tray. The verse "Qui donne moiun sou, zo zult ge aanstonds aanschouwen / Wat grafsteê, dat de tijd voor de Actieprins zal bouwen" begs a penny to reveal the tomb that Time will build for the "Actieprins" (share-prince). The card consigns the once-proud prince of speculation to the grave. Page 22 of 55.

**Pasquin's Windkaart: Ace of Hearts — Fishing for the South Sea Siren**

Ace of Hearts (heart pip, numeral "1"), titled "Eindeloos" (Endless). A speculator with a hooped net and rod tries to land a mermaid who holds a coin and clutches the empty hook. The verse "De Zuidzé Zeesieren dagt ik vergeefs te vangen, Zy knapt het geld, en laat de lege hengel hangen" has him fish in vain for the South Sea siren, who snaps up the money and leaves the line bare. The bubble is figured as a seductive but elusive siren. Page 23 of 55.

**Pasquin's Windkaart: Two of Hearts — Bubbles on Vanishing Water**

Two of Hearts (pip "2" with heart inset). A walking man holds a flaming torch and a basket of round objects (eggs or bubbles) in a landscape of cottages and a tower. The motto "Zy dryven op en onder" (they drift up and under) leads to a verse on hearts bubbling on "verdwynend Bubbel water" (vanishing bubble-water), as false "gelijk een Sater" (as a satyr). The card likens the market's rise and fall to the treacherous shenanigans of the satyr. Page 24 of 55.

**Pasquin's Windkaart: Three of Hearts — The Rich Miser, Doubly a Fool**

Three of Hearts (pip and "3"). A broad-hatted, cloaked man holds aloft a ring-and-triangle emblem in one hand and a share certificate in the other. The motto "Een ryke vrek / Is dubbeld gek" (a rich miser is doubly a fool) leads to "Hoe hoog mijn kapitaal door de Acties is gerezen, 'k Ben door mijn gierigheid niet rijker als voor dezen" — however high his capital rose through shares, his greed left him no richer. The verse pointedly parts wealth from mere capital. Page 25 of 55.

**Pasquin's Windkaart: Four of Hearts — Coin Cast to the Fishes**

Four of Hearts. A well-dressed man on a shore tosses coins into the sea, where a fish surfaces toward them. The motto "'t Gaat alles naar de zé" (it all goes to the sea) is explained by the verse: "Om al mijn geld door de Acties niet te missen; Gooi ik 't in ze, tot lokaas voor de vissen" — rather than lose his money on the shares, he throws it in as bait for the fishes. The bitter joke: feeding coin to the sea is no worse than investing it. Page 26 of 55.

**Pasquin's Windkaart: Five of Hearts — Five Senses for Sale**

Five of Hearts (heart pip and "5"). A motley-clad jester holds out a five-pointed star and a paper reading "vyf sin te koop" (five senses for sale). The verse "Ik ben niet gekker als al de and'ren… Ook hun vyf zinnen voor een Actiebrief verkopen" mocks those who, like him, sell their five senses for a share certificate. The card sharpens its point: speculators sacrifice their very reason for the promise of shares. Page 27 of 55.

**Pasquin's Windkaart: Six of Hearts — Across the Line to Ape-Land**

Six of Hearts (inset "6" with heart pip). A man holds a beam-balance with hanging scales while a tethered monkey crouches before a rising sun. The motto "Ryme Evenaar / Toont alles klaar" (the Equator shows all clearly) warns that grasping too madly at "'t Actie-werk" carries one across the Line "naar 't gloeijend Aapenland." "Aapenland" (Land of Apes) is the stock satirical destination for fools — where reckless speculation lands the greedy. Page 28 of 55.

**Pasquin's Windkaart: Seven of Hearts — The Astrologer of the Wind-Trade**

Seven of Hearts (heart pips upper left, suit emblem upper right). A robed man — "Astrologist der Windnegotie" (astrologer of the wind-trade) — peers skyward through a cross-staff toward the stars while a dog runs off behind him. The verse "Om Actie voordeel kijk ik yv'rig in de starren, Maar hoe ik meerder zie, hoe 'k meerder raak aan 't wurren" has him gaze eagerly at the stars for share-profit, only to grow more confused the more he sees. The card likens speculation to the pseudo-science of astrology. Page 29 of 55.

**Pasquin's Windkaart: Eight of Hearts — Foxes and Apes Scraping for Money**

Eight of Hearts (pip "8" and heart). A woman stands amid palm trees; a fox digs in an open chest while an ape squats beside scattered dice. The verse "'k leer Vossen en aapen / Om geld te schrapen" and "'t Is vrugteloos op winst gedagt, / Daar de Aep en Vos het voordeel wagt" warn that it is fruitless to dream of profit where fox and ape lie in wait. The card casts speculators as foxes and apes — the cunning and the uncultivated — scraping for money. Page 30 of 55.

**Pasquin's Windkaart: Nine of Hearts — Felled by the Share-Bell**

Nine of Hearts (pip and "9"). A man sprawls backward, fallen as a bell-rope snaps from a bell at upper right; a lantern lies beside him, a gabled town behind. The motto "Ai my wat smak" (alas, what a blow) leads to a verse blaming his fall on trifling "met de Actieklok" (the share-bell). The card mocks the 1720 share mania by likening it to a foolish children's game with the bell-rope — one that leaves the player flat on his back. Page 31 of 55.

**Pasquin's Windkaart: Ten of Hearts — Wind-Bubbles Sold for Nothing**

Ten of Hearts (inset heart, "10"). A seated youth in a wooded landscape blows a long clay pipe, producing a large bubble, a bowl of soap-water at his side. Titled "Windbellen om Nul te koop" (wind-bubbles sold for nothing), the verse declares "'t Is Wind en Nul en anders niet" — it is wind and naught, nothing else. The pun is exact, for the period's word for share-dealing, "windhandel," is literally "wind-trade": the card says the whole business is wind. Page 32 of 55.

**Pasquin's Windkaart: Ace of Diamonds — Samson's Riddle of the Shares**

Ace of Diamonds (single diamond pip with "I"), titled "Actie raadzel" (the shares riddle). A muscular figure — Samson — wrenches open the jaws of a lion. The verse "Nog blinder was 't geheim van de Acties, dan… 't raadzel van den dapp'ren Samson" holds the secret of the shares darker even than Samson's riddle. That riddle — "out of the eater came forth meat" (Judges 14), from the honey in the lion's carcass — was solved only by his wife's treachery; so too the shares' secret yields only to deceit. Page 33 of 55.

**Pasquin's Windkaart: Two of Diamonds — Spectacles for Blind Shareholders**

Two of Diamonds (pip and "2"). A bespectacled pedlar hawks spectacles from a tray while a bat flies overhead and an owl perches on a post. The motto "Koop brillen voor blinde Actionisten" (buy spectacles for blind shareholders) leads to a verse mocking those "die eerst in de uilevlegt hun geld en goed verkwisten" — who squandered their money in the owl's nest. The owl's nest signifies the folly and delusion of the blinded speculators. Page 34 of 55.

**Pasquin's Windkaart: Three of Diamonds — Three Cities Prop the Falling Fatherland**

Three of Diamonds (pip and "3"). A man holds a baton, his tunic bearing three escutcheons (city arms); behind him a mounted figure and a Mercury-like figure with caduceus stand on a shore. The verse "Hoe dol de wind ook gilden, Hy stuit op deze schilden" sets three cities as a bulwark that "houd de Koopgod in zijn stand, Omhelsd Neptuin, en stut het vallend Vaderland" — sustains the god of commerce and props the falling fatherland. Speculation is again likened to the capricious winds and the temperamental sea-god Neptune. Page 35 of 55.

**Pasquin's Windkaart: Four of Diamonds — South and West Struck from the Compass**

Four of Diamonds (pip and "4"). A fur-capped man on a shore holds out a mariner's compass and grips a furled flag, ships at sea. The motto "'k zoek Zuid nog West, Naar 't oosten 't best" and verse "Het Zuid en 't West heeft zo veel kwaad gedaan, Dat nooijt un naam weer op 't Kompas moest staan" declare that South and West did so much harm their names should never again stand on the compass. Ruined by the South Sea and West India schemes, the speaker turns eastward instead. Page 36 of 55.

**Pasquin's Windkaart: Five of Diamonds — The Crooked Five**

Five of Diamonds (pip "5" and single diamond). A stooped man labelled "Kromme Cinquen" writes at a table over papers, a crippled beggar on crutches behind him. The verse "De kromme Cinquen, daar ik mij op durf vertrouwen, Die zullen, vrees ik, mij in 't eind nog eens berouwen" has him trust in the "crooked five" that he fears will end in regret. The pun plays on the card's five and the crooked dealings of the share trade. Page 37 of 55.

**Pasquin's Windkaart: Six of Diamonds — Coach and Horses Blown Away**

Six of Diamonds (pip and numeral "6"). A ruined speculator stands in open country holding a worthless share certificate as empty reins slip from his hand. The caption "Daar vliegt koets en Paarden" and verse "Mijn koets en paarden zijn mij door den wind ontglipt… de teugel ook op 't laast mijn hand ontslipt" have his coach and horses carried off by the wind, the reins slipping away. The card likens the speculator to a coachman who loses control of his team, his gains blown away with them. Page 38 of 55.

**Pasquin's Windkaart: Seven of Diamonds — The Obscure Share-Book**

Seven of Diamonds (pip top right, rank "7"). A finely dressed man holds an open ledger and a sheet of paper, titled "'t Duister Actieboek" (the obscure share-book). The verse "Zo min als ik den loop der zeven hoofd Planeten Versta; zo min kan ik het eind der Actien weten" confesses that he can no more know the outcome of the shares than the course of the seven planets. Echoing the earlier astrologer card, the deck likens the share market's complexity to the unreadable heavens. Page 39 of 55.

**Pasquin's Windkaart: Eight of Diamonds — Respectability Lost to the South Sea**

Eight of Diamonds (pip "8"). A finely dressed gentleman in a long coat and wig holds a paper and a coin before a country house. The verse "Mijn Agtbaarheid is met de zuid, Door schraap- en woekerzugt verbruid" — my respectability is wedded to the South, ruined by grasping and usurious greed — turns on the motto "'k Ben de agtbaarheid, Door misdruk kwijt" (I have lost my dignity). The card stresses the dishonour that speculation brought, respectability squandered for South Sea gain. Page 40 of 55.

**Pasquin's Windkaart: Nine of Diamonds — Dreams of the Share-King**

Nine of Diamonds (pip top-right shows 9 and a diamond). A gentleman labelled "Voor den Koning" holds out a sheet of shares in one hand and a hat in the other, a country house behind. The verse "Sta ruim; want zo ik eens mag den Actie-koning raken… met Zuid en West om mijn fortuin te maken" has him dream of becoming the "Actie-koning" (share-king) by joining the South Sea and West India schemes. The card mocks the boundless ambition the speculative mania encouraged. Page 41 of 55.

**Pasquin's Windkaart: Ten of Diamonds — Who Will Buy My Last Ring?**

Ten of Diamonds (diamond pip and "10"). A ruined investor in a barren landscape holds out an empty sleeve and offers a ring, the motto "Wie koopt 'er myn laasten Ring" (who will buy my last ring). The verse "Wie stenen koopt bij nagt laat zig altoos bedotten…" warns that whoever buys precious stones by night is always deceived — as it went, it adds, with the fools at Quincampoix, the Paris street of Law's Mississippi bubble. Buying by night stands for speculating blind, the ring worthless once examined. Page 42 of 55.

**Pasquin's Windkaart: Ace of Clubs — The Pilgrim of Truth**

Ace of Clubs (single club pip, marked "1"), titled "Pelgrim van de waarheid" (Pilgrim of truth). A robed pilgrim with broad hat, staff, and a radiant sun-face emblem on his breast walks in a landscape with a tower. The verse "Ik zoek naar waarheid, en naar wysheid… ik vind de wereld even dwaas" laments that wherever he goes he finds the world equally foolish. The card broadens its satire past the share market, suggesting that greed and folly are universal human failings. Page 43 of 55.

**Pasquin's Windkaart: Two of Clubs — Empty Hands, Bare Purse**

Two of Clubs. A periwigged gentleman stands in open countryside, arms spread and pockets turned out; a small devil-like figure lurks at upper left. The verse "Ach! lege handen, kaal van beurs, en dol van hoofd… Heeft menig Actie nar van goed en bloed beroofd" — empty hands, purse bare, head gone mad — has robbed many a share-fool "of goods and blood." The exaggerated loss underscores that speculation could consume not only a fortune but reason, health, and life itself. Page 44 of 55.

**Pasquin's Windkaart: Three of Clubs — Left Hobbling on Three Legs**

Three of Clubs (pip upper-right). A stooped, bespectacled man in a cap leans on a crutch and clutches a paper share, a cottage behind him. The verse — "'k Dagt voor mijn Actie winst een heerlijk heidt te kopen / Maar, ach! zy doen in 't end my op drie beenen lopen" — mocks a speculator who thought to buy gentlemanly dignity with his share-gains but was left hobbling on three legs. The "three legs" reduce him to infirmity and dependence on a cane. Page 45 of 55.

**Pasquin's Windkaart: Four of Clubs — By Milling I Must Get It**

Four of Clubs. A fashionably dressed man strides across windswept country holding a tiny windmill aloft as cherub heads blow gusts from the clouds. The motto "Door 't malen / Moet ik 't halen" (by milling I must get it) leads to a verse: everyone now lives by winds "Die menig 't aapen land, of zijne dood doen vinden" — which lead many to Ape-Land or to their death. Chasing the empty air of speculation carries fools to the realm of apes, or to ruin. Page 46 of 55.

**Pasquin's Windkaart: Five of Clubs — Winning at Lanterloo by Cheating**

Five of Clubs (pip and "5"). A man in coat and breeches fans out playing cards in his raised hand, the other pressed to his chest. The inset "'t Gaat wel ik mijn het spel" and verse "'k Heb lanterlu, maar op een valsse wijs gekregen…" invoke the card game lanterlu (lanterloo): he has won, but by cheating, and cares nothing for others' opinion. The card satirises speculators whose fortunes rest on manipulation and luck, cut off from the society they trade in. Page 47 of 55.

**Pasquin's Windkaart: Six of Clubs — Thirst for the Share-Drink**

Six of Clubs (pip top-right). A finely dressed gentleman tips a flask to his mouth but spills it, while a small peasant points at him beside a clock-towered church. The verse "Bombario gij zijt een Guit… 'k Heb dorst naar Actidrank, maar giet myn mond juist mis" has him thirst for "Actidrank" — a pun on "actie" (shares) — yet pour it past his mouth. The card likens the greed of the share trade to a drunkard's ruinous over-indulgence. Page 48 of 55.

**Pasquin's Windkaart: Seven of Clubs — Fortune Sifted Through a Sieve**

Seven of Clubs (pip top right). A finely dressed man on a bluff holds a sieve through which coins fall to the ground, torn share certificates at his feet. The verse "'k Wierd ryk door 't Actiespel, schoon 't was een snode vond… maar 't geld bruid door de zeef… naar den grond" — I grew rich by the share-game, a wicked scheme, but the money, "the bride of fair weather," sifted away to the earth. The card marks how speculative fortune arrives and vanishes as quickly, unreliable as fair-weather love. Page 49 of 55.

**Pasquin's Windkaart: Eight of Clubs — The Eight Split into Two Zeros**

Eight of Clubs. A man labelled "Actie-agtig" (share-mad) takes a chisel to a large numeral 8 on a table, cutting it through the middle. The verse "Zo 'k de 8 door midden snij, zo hou ik maar twe nullen, Die net zo goed zijn, als de Wind-negoties prullen" leaves, once the 8 is split, only two zeros — no better than the trash of the wind-trade. The numerical joke reduces the great figure to nothing, mocking the illusion of vast fortunes conjured by speculation. Page 50 of 55.

**Pasquin's Windkaart: Nine of Clubs — Assured of Winning**

Nine of Clubs (pip "9" with a single club). A gentleman holds a blank sheet in one hand and a placard bearing concentric diamonds in the other. The motto "'k Hou voor 't dolen / Een oopen molen" precedes a verse jeering that whoever holds such a "spel" (game) need not fear loss but may be "van de winst verzekerd" — assured of winning. The promised certainty is plainly ironic: the card exposes the false confidence and self-deception of speculative investing. Page 51 of 55.

**Pasquin's Windkaart: Ten of Clubs — Blinded by the Eagle**

Ten of Clubs (inset "10" with club pip). A standing figure is beset by birds perched on head and shoulders, one a large eagle (Adelaar). The verse "De windnegotie maakte mij een halve sneês… Nu maakt mij de Adelaar en blind, en vol van vrees" — the wind-trade has made me half a man; now the Eagle leaves me blind and full of fear. The eagle, likely borne on a coin or company emblem, becomes a figure of the ruin that now terrifies rather than enriches him. Page 52 of 55.

**Pasquin's Windkaart: Title Card — The Fool's Wind-Card of 1720**

Title-page card (no suit or rank). An engraved banner held by cherubs reads "Pasquins Windkaart op de Windnegotie Van 't Iaar 1720," with a fool's pointed hat and bauble above and faces below. The verse "Prins Fredriks mantel is voor al de lauws-gezinden, Nu de eenige schuilplaats om hun veiligheid te vinden" presents the deck as a satire on the speculative wind-trade of 1720, and jests that only Prince Frederik's mantle now offers the ruined any refuge from the turmoil the bubble unleashed. Page 53 of 55.

**Pasquin's Windkaart: Closing Plate — The Money-Seeking Rooster**

Not a suited playing card but an engraved satirical plate closing the deck. A large rooster stands in a landscape, a placard ("windkaart") of grazing sheep in its beak. The caption states that "Deze nieuwe Windkaarten worden gemaakt en verkogt te Nallenstien, bij Lauthe van Scholten in den geldzoekenden Haan" — made and sold at the sign of the money-seeking Rooster. This publisher's imprint fittingly echoes the deck's theme of greed; ironically, cards condemning speculation would themselves serve the kindred risk of gambling. Page 54 of 55.

**Pasquin's Windkaart: Endpaper — Block-Printed Cover Sheet**

Not an engraved card but a sheet of decorated paper: a dense, repeating block-printed pattern of concentric rosettes formed from rings of dots in brown, black, green, and cream on a brick-red ground. No suit, rank, scene, motto, or financial subject is present; likely a binding endpaper or cover sheet of the set.

# Transcription

**Original (Dutch):**

Heer
De schop, en 't blad papier in de eene schaal gelegen,
Kan, door de Graversshoop, een goud beurs overwegen.

**English translation:**

Lord/Sir

The spade and the sheet of paper placed in one scale,
Can, through the Engraver's heap, outweigh a purse of gold.

---

**Notable markings:**

- Title at top: "Heer" (Lord/Sir)
- Spade symbol (♠) in top right corner
- Engraved illustration in woodcut or engraving style typical of 17th-century Dutch playing cards
- Text formatted as couplet/verse at bottom of card
- Part of "Pasquins Windkaart" series from "Het Groote Tafereel" (The Great Theatre)

---

# Transcription

**Original (Dutch):**

Vrouw
Men zet de schop vrij neer, ons
spelen is verbruid
De blinde razernij van Quimquampoix
heeft uit.

**English translation:**

One freely lays down the spade; our
game is ruined [lost/forfeited].
The blind frenzy of Quincampoix
has come to an end.

**Notable markings:**

- Title at top: "Vrouw" (Woman/Lady)
- Spade suit symbol (♠) in top right corner
- The text at bottom appears to be in 17th/18th century Dutch
- This is identified as "Queen of Spades" from the Pasquins Windkaart (Wind Chart) playing cards series from "Het Groote Tafereel" (The Great Theater)
- The reference to "Quimquampoix" (Quincampoix) appears to be referencing the Mississippi Bubble financial crisis

# Transcription

**Original (Dutch):**

Knegt
Prins Fredriks
mars, naar Vianen
Ik slaprins Fredriks mars, om met
al de Actiegekken .
Als wind zoldaten, naar Vrianen toe
te trekken.

**English translation:**

Prince Frederick’s
march, toward Vianen
I follow Prince Frederick’s march, together with
all the stock-mad ones.
Like wind-soldiers, to march
toward Vianen.

---

**Notable markings:**

- Title "Kauegl" at top
- Spade suit symbol (large, solid black spade) in upper right
- Engraved illustration of a figure in 17th-century dress holding a large barrel/drum, with a feathered hat
- Background landscape showing a fortified city and military encampment
- This is page 3 of the Pasquins Windkaart (Pasquin's Wind Cards) from *Het Groote Tafereel*, a Dutch satirical playing card series
- The engraving style is characteristic of Dutch woodcut/engraving from the 17th century

# Transcription

**Original (Dutch):**

Heer
Laurier Koning
k Heb de Achtes ceirst bedagt, maar een krâde Actiekans, smijt al mijn lof omver, en schent mijn lauwer krans.

**English translation:**

I first set my mind on the shares, but a poor chance in stocks
casts down all my glory and dishonors my laurel wreath.

---

**Notable markings:**

- Heart symbol containing the word "Heer" (Lord/Sir) in the upper right corner
- Border frame around the entire composition
- Historical engraving/etching style typical of 17th-century Dutch playing cards
- The figure is dressed in period clothing with elaborate decorative details
- Small cherub or putti figures visible in the background scene

# Transcription

**Original (Dutch):**

Vrouw
De Actie ketel disteleerd,
Dat het papier in Goud verkeerd
Myn Lauwersman volleerd om ieder
te bedotten,
Stookt goud uit klad papier, en
maakt't heel-al vol zotten.

**English translation:**

The stock-jobbing kettle is distilled,
so that paper is transformed into gold.
My accomplished trickster,
skilled at deceiving everyone,
boils gold out of scrap paper
and fills the whole world with fools.

---

**Notable visual elements:**

- Heart symbol (♥) in upper right corner
- Engraved portrait of an elegantly dressed woman in 18th-century attire, holding what appears to be a financial document or certificate
- Landscape background with trees and water
- Period woodcut/engraving style
- Border frame around entire composition
- This appears to be from "Pasquins Windkaart" (Pasquin's Wind Card), a satirical playing card series mocking financial speculation and the South Sea Bubble era

# Transcription

**Original (Dutch):**

Knegel of Boef
Uit Wanhoop.
Min mijn boeve hart, 't geen door een reeks van Actiestreken, Mij deed naar voordeel zien, word nu van spijt doorsteken.

**English translation:**

My rogue's heart, which through a series of stock-jobbing tricks
made me look toward profit,
is now pierced through with regret.

---

**Notable markings:**
- Heart symbol (♥) in top right corner
- Decorative border frame around entire image
- Landscape background with trees and terrain
- Figure depicted wearing 17th-century Dutch clothing with hat and holding what appears to be a heart-shaped object

# Transcription

**Original (Dutch):**

Ik ben beschermd, Heer
Daar ieder kermd.
'k Ben voor de Zuid en West hun
windgeblaas beschut
Terwijl een laauwe Goest ' Geest Heel Al
helpt in den dut.

**English translation:**

I am protected, Sir,
while everyone else laments.
I am sheltered from the South and West and their
windy blowing,
while a lukewarm spirit helps the whole world
into a doze.

---

**Notable markings:**

This is part of the "Pasquins Windkaart" (Pasquin's Wind Chart) playing cards series from *Het Groote Tafereel* (The Great Theatre). The illustration uses period engraving technique with crosshatching and line work typical of Dutch satirical prints.

By blowing too hard, the glass breaks,
just as it was with the stock bubbles

# Transcription

**Original (Dutch):**

Knegt
't Papier zo duur
Werdrook door
't vuur
Mijn Actiebrief verteend, hij kangeen
zon verdragen;
't Is vuur voor kleiner tijdj als al
de bubbelvlagen

---

**English translation:**

The paper, once so dear,
became smoke
through the fire.
My share certificate is consumed; it cannot endure
the sun.
It is fire for a shorter time than all
the bubble gusts.

**Notable markings:**

title: French Royal Tontine Certificate
description: A subscription certificate to the tenth royal tontine of France, created by royal edict in December 1759 and entered here in the eighth class. Combining engraved wording with a clerk's hand, it records that Jean Marie Joseph François Gueneau de Vauzette, a townsman of Nevers, has paid two hundred livres for a share whose annuity depends on the life of Victoire Sophie de Noailles, aged seventy-one. Joseph Micault d'Harvelay, Keeper of the Royal Treasury, issued it, and the annuity falls due twice a year. Tontines like this were a favored borrowing tool of the crown under Louis XV. Subscribers were pooled into age-classes and drew annuities that grew as fellow members died, with the last survivor inheriting the whole, so the monarchy financed itself through wagers on longevity.

pages.description: The certificate proper, headed "10.me Tontine créée par Édit du mois de Décembre 1759," eighth class. Engraved formulae filled in cursive name the subscriber Gueneau de Vauzette, the two hundred livres paid, and the nominated life, Victoire Sophie de Noailles. Dated at Paris, March 1760, with the receipt signature of the Garde du Trésor royal below. Page 1 of 2.

The verso, bearing the engraved registration clause certifying entry at the Contrôle général des Finances by its Garde des Registres, completed at Paris in September 1760 and signed by the clerk. The reverse otherwise shows only mirror-image ink bleed-through from the certificate on the recto. Page 2 of 2.

creator: Joseph Micault d'Harvelay (Garde du Trésor royal)

transcription:
# Receipt (Quittance) for a Subscription to the Tenth French Royal Tontine, Eighth Class, of the Edict of December 1759 — Transcription

## Original (French):

*(Upper-left corner, serial number:)*
**N.° 93**

*(Left margin, engraved:)*
**8e CLASSE.**
**11. Subdivisions.**

*(Engraved heading, upper right:)*
**10.me TONTINE criée par Édit du mois de Décembre 1759.**

*(Engraved body, with the secretarial hand shown in italics between the printed formulae:)*

JE JOSEPH MICAULT D'HARVELAY, Conseiller du Roi en ses Conseils, Garde de son Trésor royal, confesse avoir reçu comptant en cette ville de Paris, de *Jean Marie Joseph François Gueneau de Vauzette Bourgeois de Nevers,* pour jouir par lui, *ses heritiers et ayant cause de la rente ci-apres, sur la tête de* Mad.e *Marie Victoire Sophie De Noailles âgée de soixante unze ans,* **[veuve (?)]** *et Douairière de* M.gr *Alexandre de Bourbon Comte de Toulouse,*

la somme de

**Deux cent Livres**

en louis d'or, d'argent & monnoie, pour le principal de [blank] de rentes viagères, qui *luy* feront constituées par Messieurs les Prévôt des Marchands & Échevins de la ville de Paris, sur les trois millions de Rentes viagères dites *Tontines*, vendues & aliénées auxdits sieurs Prévôt des Marchands & Échevins, en conséquence de l'Édit du mois de Décembre 1759, registré ou besoin a été ; lesdites rentes assignées tant sur la Ferme générale des Postes que sur les droits d'Aides & Gabelles, pour jouir par *led.* *Gueneau de Vauzette* à raison d'une *[une]* action dans la *[Onzieme (?)]* de ladite rente de *[xxuij.e — chiffre incertain]* [blank] division de la *Sept.e* Classe de ladite Tontine, ensemble de la portion qu'*il* doit avoir dans les accroissemens qui surviendront par le prédécès des Rentiers de ladite *Onzieme* division de ladite *huitieme* Classe ; à commencer la jouissance du premier Janvier mil sept cent *Soixante* conformément audit Édit, & ainsi qu'il sera plus au long déclaré & énoncé par le contrat de constitution qui *luy* sera expédié de ladite Rente. De laquelle somme de *[IIc = deux cents]* à moi ordonnée pour employer au fait de ma charge [...] je me suis chargé & en quitte *led.* *Gueneau de Vauzette (?)* & tous autres.

*(Lower left, engraved line with secretarial fill:)*
Quittance du Garde du Trésor royal. Exercice mil sept cent cinquante-neuf.

*(Large flourished signature, lower right:)*
*Micault d'Harvelay* [paraphe / flourish]

*(Bottom left:)*
**M.e** *De May* **Notaire.**

*(Layout notes: engraved certificate with blanks completed in a secretarial hand; several template blanks left unfilled or filled only with a ruled line. Faint archival marks and fold/foxing throughout. The lowercase roman figure after "de ladite rente de" is not securely legible.)*

---

## English Translation:

*(Serial number:)* **No. 93**

*(Margin:)* **8th CLASS. — 11th Subdivisions.**

*(Heading:)* **10th TONTINE proclaimed by Edict of the month of December 1759.**

I, JOSEPH MICAULT D'HARVELAY, Counsellor of the King in his Councils, Keeper of his Royal Treasury, acknowledge having received in cash in this city of Paris, from *Jean Marie Joseph François Gueneau de Vauzette, burgher of Nevers,* — to be enjoyed by him, *his heirs and assigns, of the annuity hereafter, upon the life (head) of* Madame *Marie Victoire Sophie de Noailles, aged seventy-one years,* **[widow (?)]** *and Dowager of* Monseigneur *Alexandre de Bourbon, Count of Toulouse* —

the sum of

**Two hundred Livres**

in gold louis, silver and coin, for the principal of [blank] of life annuities, which shall be constituted for *him* by the Provost of the Merchants and the Aldermen of the city of Paris, upon the three millions of life annuities called *Tontines*, sold and alienated to the said Provost of the Merchants and Aldermen, in consequence of the Edict of the month of December 1759, registered where necessary; the said annuities charged both upon the General Farm of the Posts and upon the duties of Aides and Gabelles, to be enjoyed by the said *Gueneau de Vauzette* by reason of *one* share in the *[Eleventh (?)]* [subdivision], of the said annuity of *[figure uncertain]*, [in the blank] subdivision of the *Seventh* Class of the said Tontine, together with the portion he is to have in the accretions that shall arise from the predecease of the Annuitants of the said *Eleventh* subdivision of the said *Eighth* Class; the enjoyment to begin on the first of January, one thousand seven hundred *Sixty* [1760], in conformity with the said Edict, and as shall be more fully set out and stated in the deed of constitution which shall be issued to *him* for the said annuity. Of which sum of *[200]* ordered to me to employ in the business of my office [...] I have charged myself, and acquit thereof the said *Gueneau de Vauzette (?)* and all others.

*(Lower line:)* Receipt of the Keeper of the Royal Treasury. Fiscal year one thousand seven hundred fifty-nine.

*(Signature:)* *Micault d'Harvelay* [flourish]

*(Foot:)* **Maître** *De May,* **Notary.**

*(Note on conflicts: the annuitant's age is written "soixante unze" = 71, not 61 as in the guiding note (71 also fits the historical Marie Victoire Sophie de Noailles, widow of the Count of Toulouse); the subscriber is styled "Bourgeois de Nevers" [of Nevers], not of Paris as the catalogue description states; and the first class fill in the body reads "Sept.e" [7th], whereas the printed margin, the second body fill "huitieme", and the record all give the 8th Class — an internal scribal inconsistency. The notary signs "De May", not "D'Hilly".)*

title: Continental Lottery Subscriber List
description: A manuscript subscriber list with an accompanying letter for the United States (Continental) Lottery, kept by William Holliday, the lottery's agent at Winchester, Virginia, and sent on to James Searle, one of Congress's lottery managers in Philadelphia. In a tight column the sheets record each purchaser by name, the number of tickets taken, and their ticket numbers, all under the prefix "No 52," running to one hundred tickets at ten dollars each, a sum the agent totals in sterling as £375. A covering letter of 24 July 1777 remits one thousand dollars by the hand of Samuel Gilkeson. Congress ran the lottery to help pay for the Revolutionary War, and the densely filled sheet shows how briskly tickets sold in the Virginia backcountry, where buying one joined a popular flutter to the work of the cause.

pages.description: A single dense column of subscribers, each with tickets taken and ticket numbers under the prefix "No 52": John Sentz, John Abbott Esq., William Holliday, Albert Russell, Gabriel Thunker, and dozens more, holdings ranging from one to ten tickets. A running tally, "80 Carried over," is struck at the foot. Page 1 of 3.

The list concludes (Thomas Edmondson, William McClanachan, Robert Russell, and others) and is totalled: "100 Tickets @ 10 dollars each is £375." Below, a letter dated "Winchester July 24th 1777" to Mr James Searle remits 1000 dollars by Mr Samuel Gilkeson for the hundred tickets sold, signed Wm Holliday. Page 2 of 3.

The folded address leaf, directed "Mr James Searle, Philadelphia," noted "favor of Mr Gilkeson," with the remnant of a red wax seal at center and a docket at the edge reading "July 24th 1777 / William Holliday / Winchester." Page 3 of 3.

title: Continental Lottery Ticket Sales List
description: A handwritten account drawn up by Robert Traill, a local agent at Easton, Pennsylvania, recording his sales for the United States Lottery, "Class the Second." Congress authorized the lottery in 1776 to raise funds for the Revolutionary War, releasing it in successive classes through agents who carried tickets into country towns and sent the proceeds back to the commissioners in Philadelphia. The sheet lists the numbers of twenty-five tickets sold at twenty dollars each and tallies the return at five hundred dollars. Traill dated it December 27, 1778, and signed it, and it documents the mechanics of Revolutionary War finance at its smallest scale, where the new nation raised its credit one ticket at a time through a chain of named local agents.

title: United States Continental Congress Lottery Ticket, Philadelphia
description: A printed ticket for the United States Lottery, the first national lottery, which the Continental Congress authorized at Philadelphia on November 18, 1776 to raise money for the war of independence. Drawn in successive classes, the scheme paid the bearer whatever prize matched the ticket's number. The back carries later collector's notes identifying it as a Continental Lottery ticket and remarking on its rarity. Surviving tickets are exceedingly scarce, which makes this one a tangible relic of how the new union improvised its earliest finances.

title: Anglo-American Tontine Plan Prospectus
description: A printed prospectus, sent out as a banker's circular letter, proposing "A Plan of a Tontine to consist of 1000 Shares of £100 each," divided into seven age-classes whose dividends grow as members die. Shares are priced by the age of the nominee, the person whose life each share is tied to, and subscribers pay Messrs. Lockhart, bankers of Pall Mall, across the winter of 1789. What makes the scheme striking is its security: the annuities rest on United States government funds, held by London trustees, only a few years after American independence. It is a small, concrete trace of the close credit ties that already bound Britain to the young United States.

pages.description: The opening printed leaf sets out the tontine table: seven age classes with share counts, per-£100 prices, and class totals summing to £6,679. Following clauses fix the subscription deadlines, the half-yearly dividend dates, and the pledge of $600,000 in United States funds vested in the named trustees. Page 1 of 3.

The printed text continues on the left with further conditions—sale of the Three per Cent stock to cover early payments, return of subscriptions with four per cent interest if classes fail, forfeiture of unclaimed dividends, and the Dutch loan security at Amsterdam. The right bears a manuscript cover letter, "London 31 Aug.t 1789," to Messrs. Cobb & Son, Margate, soliciting their subscription, signed by Lockhart. Page 2 of 3.

The outer address leaf of the folded letter, directed in a large hand to "Mess.rs Cobb & Son, Margate," with a circular postal mark and traces of a wax seal. A docket reads "Po[st] Pa[id] Lockart, London Aug.t 31st / 1st Sept 1789." Printed lines show faintly through the paper. Page 3 of 3.

title: The Decline and Fall of the English System of Finance
description: Thomas Paine's pamphlet "The Decline and Fall of the English System of Finance," written in Paris in 1796 and reprinted in Philadelphia the same year by John Page for Benjamin Franklin Bache. Paine argues that Britain's national debt and its paper bank notes, no longer convertible to gold, are heading toward collapse on a fixed and calculable path: each war piles a new layer of debt and paper onto the last, driving down the value of the currency until the government can no longer pay in coin and the whole system ends in bankruptcy. Drawing on Adam Smith and the costs of successive wars, he forecasts the failure of the Bank of England and sets the French and English systems against each other. A convention speech on the constitution and the Declaration of Rights is appended. Paine's timing looked briefly prophetic when the Bank suspended cash payments in 1797, but his larger forecast failed: the English funding system did not collapse, and went on to finance decades more of war.

title: Proposed Lottery Scheme, London
description: A printed broadside by Jacob Henriques of London, dated April 1753, proposing a lottery of 100,000 tickets at four pounds each, drawn by sets of four figures so that 25,000 numbers decide the outcome. The scheme lays out a graded table of prizes, from twelve thousand small payouts of £10 up to four grand prizes of £10,000, together 15,272 prizes worth £394,000, with a further £6,000 set aside for the first and last tickets drawn. Henriques makes a selling point of the odds, only about five and a half losing tickets for every prize. Twelve percent would be taken from the winnings, paid in cash or government annuities, which Henriques said would go toward reducing the national debt. That public benefit was the pitch by which Henriques, one of many private schemers of the age, sought Parliament's approval for his plan.

title: States of Gelderland (Quarter of Zutphen) Redeemable Bond, Arnhem
description: A printed parchment bond of about 1647 to 1650, with its day and year completed by hand, a redeemable obligation of the Quarter of Zutphen within the province of Gelderland. It opens with the formula of Willem, Prince of Orange, as Stadholder, together with the Raden acting in the name of the Heeren Staten, and recites a resolution taken at the Landdag held at Zutphen in April 1644. It invokes the late Frederick Henry, Prince of Orange, described as of laudable memory and in life also Stadholder, father of our Stadholder, which places the actual issue after his death in March 1647. The body promises to pay interest on the principal at six per hundred yearly, from year to year, until redemption, securing both capital and interest, the sum reckoned in guilders of twenty stivers each. It was given at Arnhem and sealed with the great seal, countersigned by the Court's clerk.
creator: Prince of Orange-Nassau (Willem / Frederick Henry)
notes: Archaic Dutch princely bond/obligation. "Y VVILHELM BY DER GRATIE GODES, Prince van [?]..." References FREDERICUS HENRICX (Frederick Henry), Prince of Orange. Tresorier General and Rentmeester noted. Mid-17th century Dutch Golden Age fiscal document.
transcription:
# Redeemable Bond of the States of Gelderland (Quarter of Zutphen), Arnhem, 1648 — Transcription

## Original:

(Printed archaic Dutch on parchment; a large ornamental woodcut initial fills the upper-left corner. Blanks left in the printed text are filled in by hand — these handwritten insertions are shown here {in curly braces}. Handwriting is difficult; uncertain readings are marked [?] or [illegible].)

**(large ornamental woodcut initial at left)**

**VVILHELM, BY DER GRATIE GODES,**
Printze van Oraignen, &c. Stadtholder, mitsgaders die Raeden uyt den naem van de Heeren Staten des Vor-
stendoms Gelre ende Graefschaps Zutphen, Doen condt in crachte deses, Alsoo 't den wel gedachten Heeren Staeten belieft heeft te resolvieren
op den Lantdach in April 1644 binnen de Stadt Zutphen gehouden, by advijs ende uytsprake van Sijne Hoogheyt, den oock Doorluch-
tigen en Hooghgebooren Vorst ende Heere **FREDERIJCK HENRIJCK,** Printze van Oraignen, &c. Hooghloflijcker memorie,
in leven mede Stadholder, Heer Vader van ons Sadtholder, gedatiert den 13/25 vande voornoemde Maent Aprilis, datmen tot meesten wel-
stant ende reddinghe van den voorsz: Vorstendom ende Graeffschap by jegenwoordige gelegentheyt, doen lichten ende op Interesse negotieren
sal seeckere sommen van penningen, om bekeert ende geemployeert te worden, tot betalinge van der Landtschaps nootelijcke schulden ende
lasten, naerder verhaelt by de voorsz: uytspraecke, ende de voornoemde Resolutie daer op gevolght vande wel gemelde Heeren Staten. Soo
bekennen wy in krachte deses dat {Evert[?] van Beckhoven[?] tot [Cletelborst?]} op huyden dato onderschreven in goeden ganckbaren
gelde, ten behoeve van welgedachte Heeren Staten getelt ende gelevert heeft de somma van {ses hondert vijftich gulden} tot
twintich stuyvers 't stuck. Ende willende mits dien de voorn: {Evert van Beckhoven[?]} sijn erven, ofte Actie van {[geen?]} hebbende
behoorlijck bewaren, Hebben wy in name van welghedachte Heeren Staten, uyt krachte van de voornoemde resolutie van hare Ed: Mog: inhererende de voorghemelde uyt-
spraecke, belooft en beloven mits desen die vooraengetogene summa van {ses hondert vijftich gulden} te verrenten met ses en een oort ten hondert, maeckende jaerlijcx
{veertich guldens[?] ...} te betalen van jaer tot jaer, daer van 't eerste jaer verscheenen sal zijn op den {xvj·[?] [maand — illegible]} des naestvolgende jaers {[illegible handwritten date]}
{[illegible]} ende soo voorts van jaer tot jaer, tot d'aflossinge toe. Daer op wy verseeckeren de voorn: {Evert van Beckhoven[?]}, soo voor 't Capitael als Interesse, mitsgaders
d'onkosten, die by gebreck van prompte betalinge op de voorsz: termijnen, of veerthien dagen daer na onbegrepen tot taxatie van den Hove, na gedane maninge soude mogen com-
men te loopen. Verbindende daer voor alle die gemeyne middelen, Imposten, Verpondingen, ende Comptoiren van ontfange van den voorn: Vorstendom ende Graeffschap,
gheen uytgesondert, ende een voor al, tot verwaringe ende schadeloos holdinge van de voornoemde {Evert van Beckhoven[?] sijn} Erven ofte actie van {[geen?]} heb-
bende, om die selve voor den Hove gedachtes Vorstendoms ende Graeffschaps, in val van misbetalinge, by reele executie te vervolgen, tot effective betalinge toe, sonder dat daer
tegens sal worden gedaen, ofte toegelaten eenighsins gedaen te worden. Tot welcken eynde mits desen van alle exceptien ende beneficien van rechten gerenuncieert wort, Mits
dat soo wel aen d'een als d'ander zijde vry sal staen, soo wel die loesse te doen als 't Capitael wederom te vorderen; Invoegen nochtans dat 't versoeck ende opkondige van de losse
respective een half jaer te vooren gheschiede. Ende dat in sulcken val, als oock vande rente die betalinge gedaen sal worden met goeden ganckbaren ende gepermitteerden gelde.
Willende dat desen onsen brief, Vidimus ofte Copie authentijcq, mitsgaders assignatie op eenigh Comptoir des voornoemden Vorstendoms ende Graeffschap van ons, voor d'eerste
reyse met quitantie, ende daer na quitantie alleenlijck, soo dickwils als 't van nooden sal zijn over gebracht wesende, die betalinge aenden voorn: {Evert van Beckhoven[?]}
geschieden sal, welcke betalinge den Lantrentmeester generael gedachtes Vorstendoms ende Graeffschaps, ofte dien sulcx anders te laste geleyt sal mogen wesen, in uytgave sonder
swarigheyt sal worden geleden; Alles sonder argh of list; In oorkonde hebben wy 't groote Segel gedachtes Vorstendoms ende Graeffschaps onder jegenwoordige verschryvinge
laten hangen, ende deselve door des Hoves Griffier doen beteeckenen. **Gegeven t'Arnhem den** {xvj·[?] [maand — illegible] xvjᶜ· [achtenveertich? = 1648]}
