notes: Belgian/French company document, Extrait des Statuts (corporate statutes extract) in French; references to Louis Lambert, general assembly in Brussels, dividends and board of directors; p.1/2
transcription:
# Extract of the Statutes of the Société de l'Ikelemba — Transcription

## Original:

(Printed extract set within an ornamental engraved border with scrolled corner flourishes; a faint intaglio image shows through from the reverse. The text is arranged in two columns beneath a centered display heading.)

**EXTRAIT DES STATUTS**

(small ornament — ⋇ — beneath the heading)

*(Left column:)*

**ARTICLE PREMIER.** — Il est constitué, par les présentes, une société anonyme sous la dénomination de L'Ikelemba.

**ART. 2.** — La Société a son siège social au Congo (Etat Indépendant), dans le bassin de l'Ikelemba, et son siège administratif en Belgique, à Bruxelles ou dans l'agglomération bruxelloise.

Elle pourra avoir des sièges administratifs en tous autres pays où s'exercera son industrie ou son commerce.

**ART. 3.** — La Société est fondée pour une durée de trente ans, mais elle peut prendre des engagements et acquérir des concessions pour un terme excédant cette durée.

Celle-ci pourra être prolongée ou réduite comme il sera dit à l'article 34 des présents statuts.

**ART. 5.** — Le capital social est fixé à 500,000 francs, représenté par 5,000 actions de capital de 100 francs chacune.

Il est, en outre, créé 5,000 actions de dividende sans désignation de valeur.

M. Louis Lamberts, prénommé, fait apport à la Société de l'Ikelemba du droit d'acquérir, pour elle, un bloc de 1,000 hectares de terres, dont la propriété a été demandée par lui et dont les comparants déclarent avoir connaissance, à déterminer dans le bassin de l'Ikelemba.

En rémunération de cet apport, il lui est attribué les deux dixièmes des actions de dividende.

Les 4,000 actions de dividende restantes sont attribuées aux souscripteurs, ci-après, des 5,000 actions de capital, proportionnellement à leur souscription.

Toutes les actions de dividende sont inaliénables pendant les deux premières années après la date des présentes, à moins d'une autorisation expresse du Conseil d'administration.

Le nombre des actions de dividende ne pourra jamais être augmenté, pas même par voie de modification aux statuts.

*(Right column:)*

**ART. 30.** — Les assemblées générales se réunissent à Bruxelles ou dans l'un de ses faubourgs, au lieu désigné par le Conseil d'administration.

L'assemblée générale annuelle se tient le dernier samedi de juin de chaque année, à 3 heures de relevée.

La première assemblée générale annuelle aura lieu en 1900.

**ART. 37.** — Au 31 décembre de chaque année, et pour la première fois le 31 décembre 1899, les livres de la Société sont arrêtés et le Conseil d'administration dresse le bilan.

**ART. 41.** — L'excédent favorable du bilan, déduction faite de tous les frais généraux, constitue le bénéfice de la Société ; ce bénéfice sera réparti comme suit :

1. 5 p. c. pour la réserve légale, jusqu'à ce qu'elle ait atteint la dixième partie du capital social ;

Le Conseil d'administration pourra augmenter cette réserve et, en outre, créer une réserve spéciale ou un fonds de prévision ;

2. Un premier dividende de 5 p. c. sur la partie appelée des actions de capital, dans le cas où les bénéfices nets d'une année ne seraient pas suffisants pour payer ce dividende aux actions de capital ; la somme qui manquera sera prélevée, sans intérêts de retard, sur les bénéfices des années subséquentes, après dotation de la réserve légale.

Le solde se répartit comme suit :

2 p. c. à chaque administrateur et à chaque commissaire un tiers du tantième revenant à chaque administrateur.

Le minimum à attribuer à chaque administrateur et à chaque commissaire est réservé à la décision de l'assemblée générale, qui se tiendra immédiatement après la constitution de la Société.

Le surplus sera distribué par moitié aux actions de capital et par moitié aux actions de dividende.

(A decorative scrolled flourish is printed below the two columns, centered.)

---

## English Translation:

**EXTRACT OF THE STATUTES**

*(Left column:)*

**ARTICLE ONE.** — There is hereby constituted, by these presents, a joint-stock company (société anonyme) under the name of L'Ikelemba.

**ART. 2.** — The Company has its registered office in the Congo (Independent State), in the basin of the Ikelemba, and its administrative seat in Belgium, at Brussels or in the Brussels agglomeration.

It may have administrative offices in any other countries where it carries on its industry or its commerce.

**ART. 3.** — The Company is founded for a term of thirty years, but it may enter into commitments and acquire concessions for a term exceeding this duration.

The latter may be extended or reduced as shall be stated in article 34 of the present statutes.

**ART. 5.** — The share capital is fixed at 500,000 francs, represented by 5,000 capital shares of 100 francs each.

There are, moreover, created 5,000 dividend shares without par value.

Mr. Louis Lamberts, named above, contributes to the Société de l'Ikelemba the right to acquire, for it, a block of 1,000 hectares of land, the ownership of which has been applied for by him and of which the appearing parties declare they have knowledge, to be determined in the basin of the Ikelemba.

In remuneration for this contribution, there are allotted to him two-tenths of the dividend shares.

The remaining 4,000 dividend shares are allotted to the subscribers, hereafter, of the 5,000 capital shares, in proportion to their subscription.

All dividend shares are inalienable during the first two years after the date of these presents, unless by express authorization of the Board of Administration.

The number of dividend shares may never be increased, not even by way of amendment to the statutes.

*(Right column:)*

**ART. 30.** — General meetings are held at Brussels or in one of its suburbs, at the place designated by the Board of Administration.

The annual general meeting is held on the last Saturday of June of each year, at 3 o'clock in the afternoon.

The first annual general meeting shall take place in 1900.

**ART. 37.** — On December 31 of each year, and for the first time on December 31, 1899, the books of the Company are closed and the Board of Administration draws up the balance sheet.

**ART. 41.** — The favorable surplus of the balance sheet, after deduction of all general expenses, constitutes the profit of the Company; this profit shall be distributed as follows:

1. 5 percent for the legal reserve, until it has reached one-tenth of the share capital;

The Board of Administration may increase this reserve and, in addition, create a special reserve or a contingency fund;

2. A first dividend of 5 percent on the called-up portion of the capital shares, in the case where the net profits of a year would not be sufficient to pay this dividend to the capital shares; the amount that is lacking shall be drawn, without interest for arrears, from the profits of subsequent years, after endowment of the legal reserve.

The balance is distributed as follows:

2 percent to each administrator and to each auditor, one-third of the share accruing to each administrator.

The minimum to be allotted to each administrator and to each auditor is reserved to the decision of the general meeting, which shall be held immediately after the constitution of the Company.

The surplus shall be distributed one-half to the capital shares and one-half to the dividend shares.

pages.description: Printed extract of the statutes (Extrait des Statuts) of an anonymous joint-stock company, the Société de l'Ikelemba, set in French in two columns within an ornamental engraved border. Article 1 constitutes the société anonyme; Article 2 fixes its registered office in the Congo (État Indépendant du Congo), in the Ikelemba river basin, with an administrative seat at Brussels. The capital is set at 500,000 francs, divided into 5,000 capital shares of 100 francs each, alongside 5,000 dividend (founders') shares of no par value. Louis Lamberts contributes the company's right to acquire some 1,000 hectares of land in the Ikelemba basin, receiving two-tenths of the dividend shares in return. The first financial year closes 31 December 1899 and the first annual general meeting is to be held in 1900, dating the constitution to 1899. The text reflects the concession-company model by which Leopold II's Congo Free State licensed private syndicates to exploit equatorial land and produce. The restrained typographic frame, with scrolled corner flourishes and no allegorical imagery, presents the venture as a sober legal instrument rather than a speculative prospectus.

This is the dividend-coupon sheet (the second of two pages) belonging to a share in a Belgian société anonyme operating in the Congo, the company recorded on its companion certificate. Thirty coupons, numbered 1 to 30 and arranged in three columns of ten, each sit within an ornamental engraved cartouche; all remain blank, neither dated nor filled with an amount, so the share was never cut for payment. The sheet embodies the mechanics of dividend distribution in the era before bank book-entry: each numbered slip was to be detached and surrendered in turn as successive dividends fell due, a paper ledger of the shareholder's future claims. The flowing, asymmetric foliate scrollwork framing each number, with its whiplash curves, reflects the Art Nouveau idiom then fashionable in Brussels, lending an artisanal elegance to an otherwise utilitarian instrument of colonial finance.

pages.description: A printed receipt (kwitantie) of the Amsterdam banking house Lippmann, Rosenthal & Co., acknowledging that it has taken over ("overgenomen") from Heer Burdet, Druyvestejn the talons of 3 per cent. bonds of the Grand Russian Railway Company (Groote Russische Spoorweg Maatschappij), third emission of 1881, the talon values noted at Rb. 125 and Rb. 625. Issued at Amsterdam on 12 June 1924. The talon, the stub from which a fresh sheet of interest coupons was drawn once the old sheet was exhausted, here passes through an Amsterdam intermediary years after the 1917 revolution had repudiated Russia's foreign railway debt. A green admonition urges that the receipt be kept "voor eene eventueele afstempeling," and an older stamp records a coupon paid 1/14 June 1917, the dual date marking the gulf between the Julian and Gregorian calendars. The document is a small relic of Dutch holders still administering Russian securities whose value the new regime had already disowned.

This is the reverse of a printed receipt issued at Amsterdam by the banking house Lippmann, Rosenthal & Co., the firm having handled the renewal of interest coupons (talons) on 3 percent bonds of the Grand Russian Railway Company. The back carries only two markings: a boxed cancellation stamp reading "OORSPRONKELIJKE KWITANTIE AFGETEEKEND. L. R. & Co." ("original receipt signed off") and, in green, the formula "AAN DEN INHOUD VOLDAAN" ("satisfied as to the contents") above a place-and-date line "AMSTERDAM, 19[—]" left blank. The document speaks to Amsterdam's role as a clearing centre for Russian railway securities held by Dutch investors, where a bank's stamp converted a promise into a settled account. The near-empty field, a mere acknowledgement of payment, marks the quiet administrative end of a cross-border credit relationship.

title: Hoogheemraadschap van den Lekdijk Bovendams Rentebrief
description: An allonge of 1944, a coupon-renewal sheet appended to a rentebrief, the perpetual annuity bond of the Hoogheemraadschap van den Lekdijk Bovendams, the water board charged with maintaining the upper Lek river dike. It was issued at Utrecht on 8 January 1944 and authenticated by the Dijkgraaf and Secretaris. The underlying obligation, drawn on a principal of one thousand guilders, yields twenty-five guilders annually, a rate of 2.5 percent, payable each year on 12 January. The sheet exists because the original coupons were exhausted: its body is a dense ledger of redeemed interest, the lettered entries running from January 1944 to 2003.

pages.description: This heavily worn manuscript is a Dutch interest-bearing obligation, an obligatie or redeemable annuity (losrente), penned in an abbreviated notarial hand on heavy paper or parchment. The dense early-eighteenth-century Dutch body records a debt carrying fixed yearly interest of twenty-five guilders, payable each 12 January, and is subscribed by several parties, among them a Nicolaes and one styled van Roossbergh. Its true substance lies in the margins, where a long column of dated receipts logs that annual payment year after year: the entries run from 1703 down through the 1720s and onward across the head and right edge into the early 1780s. Issued around 1702 to 1703, the instrument testifies to the durability of the Dutch credit market, where such annuities passed between holders and quietly yielded their coupon for the better part of a century. Plain and unornamented, the sheet speaks not through emblem but through its accreted ledger of fidelity: a market that paid on the same January day for some eighty years.

This is the verso of an early modern Dutch manuscript obligation (obligatie), a registered debt instrument written by hand on folded vellum. The recto carries the body of the bond and its principal terms; the back, shown here, is given over entirely to the document's administrative afterlife. Fold lines divide the skin into a grid, and within that grid clerks have packed columns of dated entries — interest payments received, transfers of title from one holder to the next, and marginal reckonings — alongside a central inscribed block that appears to record an assignment of the bond. Such a verso is the working ledger of a security that changed hands repeatedly, and it speaks to the depth of the Dutch market for transferable debt: a single obligation could circulate among investors for decades, each endorsement extending its life. The dense, accreted hands make most individual entries illegible in the scan.

A central red-bordered cartouche names the value, one guan, or a thousand copper cash, and below it the woodblock depicts ten strings of a hundred coins, rendering that sum to the eye. Flanking columns declare the note current throughout the realm and warn that counterfeiters will be executed and informers rewarded with the offender's property. It is printed on coarse mulberry-bark paper and struck with vermilion seals. It is among the largest paper notes ever issued and the oldest paper currency to survive in quantity. pages.description: A one-guan note of the Great Ming Circulating Treasure Note (大明通行寶鈔), the fiat paper money issued by the Ministry of Revenue (戶部) under the Hongwu Emperor from 1375. A central red-bordered cartouche names the value — 壹貫, one guan, or a thousand copper cash — and below it the woodblock depicts ten strings of a hundred coins, rendering that sum to the eye for an often-illiterate public; flanking columns declare the note current throughout the realm and warn that counterfeiters will be executed and informers rewarded with the offender's property. Printed on coarse mulberry-bark paper and struck with vermilion seals, it is among the largest paper notes ever issued and the oldest paper currency to survive in any quantity. It is also a parable of fiat money: unbacked and relentlessly over-printed, the notes lost almost all their worth — trading by the 1420s at a tiny fraction of face value — until the Ming gave up paper and China returned to silver for centuries.

The verso of a Ming-dynasty paper note, the Da Ming Tong Xing Bao Chao (大明通行寶鈔), the empire-wide circulating treasure certificate issued under imperial monopoly by the Ministry of Revenue (戶部). Printed by woodblock on coarse grey mulberry-fibre paper, this back carries no text of its own: the dark rectangular impression at the top is the bleed-through of the framed face design, while the substance of the side is a large vermilion official seal stamped near the lower centre, the mark of state authorization that gave the note its standing. Denominated on the front at one guan (貫, nominally a string of one thousand copper cash), the issue belongs to the great Ming experiment in pure fiat currency begun in the Hongwu reign. Unbacked by metal and printed without redating across reign-years, such notes depreciated steadily as issue outran demand, and the worn, near-effaced surface here testifies to long, hard circulation of an over-printed money.

title: United States (Continental) Lottery Ticket, Philadelphia
description: A printed bearer ticket for the United States Lottery, marked "CLASS the FIRST," entitling its holder to receive whatever prize was drawn against its number under a resolution of Congress passed at Philadelphia on November 18, 1776. The lottery manager D. Jackson signed it by hand. The Continental Congress created the lottery by that resolution to help pay for the Revolutionary War, running it in successive classes of tickets that promised cash prizes drawn by lot. Because whoever held the ticket could claim its prize, it worked much like a public subscription, turning the patriotic gamble of ordinary buyers into wartime revenue for the government.
creator: D. Jackson (lottery manager)

title: South Sea Annuities Dividend Warrant
description: A printed dividend warrant, filled in by hand, issued at South Sea House on April 30, 1730. It authorizes payment of half a year's annuity to a named holder out of the South Sea Annuities, the fund Parliament created when it split the company's capital in two and converted one half into annuities for the company's members. The warrant fixes the holding at a 4 percent rate, due at the quarter day, with a printed instruction to sign a receipt on the back. The company's officers authorized it, and it documents the routine servicing of the South Sea Company's reorganized debts in the decade after the Bubble.

title: Antwerp Exchange Obligation, Generale Keyserlyke Indische Compagnie
description: A Dutch obligation, printed and completed by hand, issued at Antwerp Exchange. It records a forward contract for shares in the Imperial Ostend Company, chartered under Habsburg authority. The signer, acting as a profit-agent, binds himself and his goods to deliver and pay for the shares on an appointed day of transfer against a cash premium, and the contract sets terms for repaying legitimate costs, paying dividends, and answering for any failure to deliver. An engraved Imperial coat of arms crowns the sheet, a mark of the Habsburg charter under which the company traded with the Indies until diplomatic pressure forced its suspension in 1727.

title: Alexander Hamilton Treasury Circular on Subscription of State Debt Certificates
description: A manuscript circular headed "Treasury Department Oct. 13. 1790" and signed "A. Hamilton," carrying a ruling from the Secretary of the Treasury to the commissioners of loans. Hamilton reports that one commissioner had read the law narrowly, supposing that certificates of state debt could not be subscribed to the new federal loans unless they expressly stated they were issued for services or supplies toward the late war. Hamilton rejects that reading: it would exclude every certificate that merely acknowledges a sum due, along with all certificates for money loaned to the states, which was not the law's intent. Where a certificate appears, from its wording or from public records, to have been issued for wartime expenditures and the defense of the United States, the commissioners are to accept it. Written as the federal government took on the states' debts under the Funding Act of 1790, the letter shows Hamilton settling, case by case, the eligibility rules that would fold scattered state obligations into a single funded federal debt.
creator: Alexander Hamilton (Secretary of the Treasury)
notes: Alexander Hamilton circular letter, Treasury Department, October 13, 1795. On eligibility of state debt certificates for subscription to new federal loans under the Funding Act of 1790.
transcription:
# Transcription

**Treasury Department Oct 13 1795**

(Circular)

Sir,

I find from a letter from one of the Commissioners of Loans, that it is conceived, certificates of the State Debts cannot be subscribed to the new Loans unless that they express that they are issued for services or supplies towards the prosecution of the late war.—

By this construction all certificates containing a simple acknowledgement of debt to a certain amount and all Certificates for monies loaned to the States would be excluded which is not the intent and meaning of the laws. If a Certificate of any State shall be issued and it shall not appear by the tenor of it, if it cannot be ascertained from any public record act or document to have been issued for some purpose, other than common transactions and expenditures for forces or supplies towards the prosecution of the late war and the defence of the United States, or some part thereof during the said war, it is consistent with the directions of the law to receive it on loan.—

I am Sir

Your Obedient Servant

**A Hamilton**

---

**Notable markings:**

- Signature: "A Hamilton" (Alexander Hamilton)
- Document classification: "(Circular)" - indicating this is a circular letter distributed to multiple recipients
- Date: October 13, 1795
- Header: "Treasury Department"

title: Massachusetts Bills of Exchange Schedule
description: A handwritten accounting schedule headed "Massachusetts," listing bills of exchange drawn for that state and signed at Philadelphia on September 22, 1778 by Thomas Hopkinson of the loan office. Ten denominations from $12 to $1,200 are set against the number of sets and their running serial ranges, each row giving its amount in dollars, and the columns total 1,803 sets worth $93,000. The Continental Congress produced records like this as part of its wartime effort to fund the war through loan-office certificates and bills payable abroad, and the schedule captures the fine-grained bookkeeping by which the states' shares of a common debt were divided up, denomination by denomination, before the bills entered circulation.

title: Rowley, Massachusetts Selectmen's Fine Warrant
description: A handwritten warrant of the selectmen of Rowley, Massachusetts, dated August 15, 1782, directing Constable Samuel Searl to collect from each person on the attached list his share of the fine levied on the town's Sixth Class "for not procuring a man to Serve in the Continental Army." Five selectmen signed it: Thomas Mighill, Daniel Spofford, Joseph Poor, Joshua Pickard, and Isaac Smith. The warrant reflects a Massachusetts wartime practice under which a town's men were sorted into classes, each class bound either to furnish a soldier or to pay an assessment in place of service. Here the fine falls on the class as a whole, divided among its members, rather than on any single man who failed to serve.

title: State of Massachusetts-Bay War Bond issued to Seth Davenport
description: A printed and manuscript bond of the State of Massachusetts Bay, dated February 26, 1777, acknowledging twenty pounds in lawful money borrowed from Seth Davenport for the use and service of the state. The treasurer promises to repay the principal by June 1, 1780, in Spanish milled dollars at six shillings each, or in coined silver and gold valued by an earlier colonial act of 1749, with interest at six percent paid each year. Massachusetts issued the bond to help fund the Revolutionary War, and it is a direct emission of state debt of the kind later assumed and consolidated into the federal debt. The back carries endorsements recording its settlement in the following decade.

title: Dutch Bond for the French Bourbon Princes in Exile
description: This printed Dutch obligation, worth one thousand guilders, records a share in a loan that the exiled Bourbon princes raised on the Amsterdam market in September 1793. It was issued from their court-in-exile at Hamm in Westphalia by the Comte de Provence and the Comte d'Artois, the brothers of Louis XVI, months after his execution. Strikingly, the loan was raised not in their own names but in the name of "the King" — their nephew, the boy whom royalists had recognized as Louis XVII, then held prisoner in Paris and dead within two years. Amsterdam bankers acknowledge receipt of the capital, and the issue is capped at twelve thousand shares. Coming while Republican France and the émigrés were at war, the bond shows the counter-revolution financed through Amsterdam's money market, its royal language intact even though the throne it invoked had fallen.
creator: Louis Stanislas Xavier (Comte de Provence); Charles Philippe (Comte d'Artois); J. Bourcourd & Wedowe F. Croese & Comp. (Amsterdam)

title: Russian Imperial Treasury Note
description: A short-term Treasury note of the Imperial Russian State Treasury for fifty rubles, dated 1915 and paying 4 percent a year. Printed in green and black, it declares itself valid until August 1, 1929, and carries a column of four detachable coupons at the left, numbered five through eight and worth one ruble each, covering the semi-annual interest payments due between 1918 and 1919. It bears the double-headed imperial eagle and the signatures of the Manager of the State Treasury, the Director, and a bookkeeper. The Imperial government issued notes like this to fund itself as the First World War deepened its deficits. This one would not mature until 1929, by which time the regime that printed it had long since fallen.

title: Kingdom of Greece Guaranteed Gold Loan Bond, Athens
description: A bearer bond of the Kingdom of Greece, issued for its gold-guaranteed loan of 1898, with a face value of 2,500 gold drachmas and a coupon of 2½ percent. Printed in Athens and authenticated in London, it carries the signature of the Greek Minister of Finance and a countersignature for the Bank of England, which served as the loan's paying agent. The loan followed a run of disasters for Greek public finance: a default on the national debt in 1893, then defeat in the 1897 war with the Ottoman Empire. In response, Greece's finances were placed under an International Financial Commission, and the loan was floated under the joint guarantee of France, Britain, and Russia. That guarantee is the document's real subject. It is what let Greece borrow at a coupon as low as 2½ percent, and it is why the bond, for all the Hellenic splendor of its engraved frame and royal arms, records a treasury placed under outside control.
creator: Kingdom of Greece (Ministry of Finance); guaranteed by Bank of England

title: Romania National Defense Fund Army Equipment Bond (Bon pentru Înzestrarea Armatei), Bucharest
description: A four percent bond of 500 lei issued in 1940 by Romania's Autonomous Administration of the National Defense Fund, under the title "Bond for the Equipping of the Army." Authorized by the Council of Ministers in February 1940, it was to be repaid at full value on March 1, 1945, and its principal and interest were exempted from every present and future tax, due, and state or local levy, a sweetener meant to draw subscribers to an urgent cause. Romania issued it at Bucharest to fund a rushed rearmament drive as the kingdom braced against mounting pressure on its borders. Within months that pressure took concrete form: Romania lost Bessarabia to the Soviet Union and northern Transylvania to Hungary, ceding both without the fight the bond was raising money to prepare for. The certificate is a deliberate showpiece, designed by the painter Gheorghe Chirovici in an emphatically national style: folk-revival interlace and grapevine borders, the royal arms beneath a crown, and three vignettes of a gun crew, a tank, and a military aircraft, picturing the modernization of the three services the loan was meant to equip.

title: American & British Securities Company Common Stock Certificate, Delaware
description: A share certificate for one hundred shares of common stock in the American & British Securities Company, a corporation organized under the laws of Delaware. The shares are issued "without nominal or par value," a form still relatively new in 1923 that the printed text takes care to explain, and the face is overprinted with the word COMMON in bold red, set diagonally to distinguish it from the company's preferred stock. The certificate sets out the basic terms of that two-class structure: each share, common or preferred, carries one vote at stockholders' meetings, while preferred holders take priority in dividends. Dated 1923 and signed by its president and secretary, it belongs to the wave of Anglo-American investment holding companies chartered after the First World War, when Delaware's permissive corporate law and the tightening financial ties between London and New York encouraged such vehicles. Its restrained steel-engraved border follows the conventional banknote manner, signaling security and probity rather than any particular artistic aim.

# Transcription

**No. 18                                                                                                           100 Shares**

## AMERICAN & BRITISH SECURITIES COMPANY
INCORPORATED UNDER THE LAWS OF THE STATE OF DELAWARE.

This Certifies that **Hattie J. Barnhill**

is the owner of **ONE HUNDRED (100)** shares of COMMON STOCK of AMERICAN & BRITISH SECURITIES COMPANY, each share without nominal or par value, fully paid and non-assessable, transferable only on the books of the corporation, in person or by attorney, upon the surrender of this certificate properly endorsed.

The holders of preferred stock are entitled to receive on or before the first day of each annum, payable semi-annually in each year, at such times as the board of Directors shall determine, and which said dividends shall be in preference to and shall be payable before any dividends shall be apart on paid upon the common stock. The dividends due upon the preferred stock semi-annually from the date of issue to and including September 15th, 1919, shall not be cumulative, but thereafter, to-wit, after September 15th, 1919, dividends at the rate of seven per cent. (7%) per annum on any deficiency in any of the dividends to be paid on the preferred stock on or before October 15th, 1919, shall be made good out of the earnings of subsequent years before dividends shall be paid upon the common stock.

In the event of a dissolution or liquidation of the corporation or a voluntary or involuntary, or upon any distribution of its capital, there shall be paid to the holders of the preferred stock the par value thereof, to wit, one hundred dollars ($100) per share, and also any assets distributed among the holders of the common stock, after payment to the holders of the preferred stock of its accrued and unpaid, accrued and accumulated dividends as above provided, the remaining funds of the corporation shall be divided among and paid to the holders of the common stock, according to the shares held by each respectively.

The corporation shall have the option of redeeming the preferred stock, in whole or in part, at any time after issue, on any semi-annual dividend period, by payment to the holders thereof of the sum of one hundred dollars ($100) per share for each share of such preferred stock so redeemed, together with all accrued and accumulated dividends thereon, upon thirty days actual or published notice to the holders thereof.

Each share of preferred stock and each share of common stock outstanding shall be entitled to one vote each at all meetings of stockholders for any purpose. The common stock shall have no nominal or par value, and each share of the same shall be entitled in the event of the sale or other disposition of all or substantially all of the assets of the corporation to vote thereon, subject to the payment of all sums due and payable upon the preferred stock, cumulative or non-cumulative according to their nature.

IN WITNESS WHEREOF, the corporation has caused this certificate to be signed by its duly authorized officers, and its corporate seal to be hereunto affixed this _____ day of _____________, 19___.

**Edward P. Johnson**                                                                                              [illegible signature]

title: Act of Parliament, 8 George I (1722): paying off Exchequer Bills and ease to the South-Sea Company
description: A printed Act of the Parliament of Great Britain from the eighth year of the reign of George I, printed at London in 1722 by John Baskett, the King's Printer. An act for paying off and canceling one million pounds of Exchequer Bills and for "giving ease" to the South Sea Company, it ranks among the principal financial measures enacted after the collapse of the South Sea scheme in 1720. Its many clauses reach across the whole business of the state: they provide for exchanging Exchequer Bills against the Sinking Fund, regulate the dealings of the South Sea and East India Companies, charge the South Sea Company with annuities, set penalties for counterfeiting bills, and appropriate supplies for the army, navy, garrisons, and Chelsea Hospital. Others range further still, granting debentures to the planters of Nevis and St. Christopher and laying new duties on imported apples and pictures. The royal arms and King's Printer imprint mark it as an official statute of the realm.

pages.description: Title page: "Anno Regni GEORGII REGIS Magnae Britanniae, Franciae, & Hiberniae OCTAVO," with the royal arms and "G R" cypher. London, printed by John Baskett, 1722. Page 1 of 37.

This leaf is the blank verso of the title page of a printed volume of the Acts of Parliament of Great Britain, gathered for the eighth year of the reign of King George I ("Anno Regni Georgii Regis... Octavo"). Nothing is printed on this side; what one sees is the recto's letterpress showing through in mirror image, a familiar artefact of impression on hand-laid rag paper. The reversed text records that the Parliament was begun at Westminster on the seventeenth day of March 1714, in the first year of the reign, and continued by prorogations to the nineteenth of October 1721, the eighth session. The imprint names John Baskett, printer to the King's most excellent Majesty, with the assigns of Thomas Newcomb and Henry Hills, London, 1722, the date the volume was printed. The royal arms, bearing the motto "Dieu et mon droit," appear faintly through the sheet. Such sessional volumes made the realm's statutes public, the legal scaffolding within which Crown finance, chartered trade, and the post-South-Sea credit settlement operated.

title: Anno Regni Georgii II Regis Vicesimo Quarto: An Act for raising money by Exchequer Bills to pay off the South Sea Annuities
description: A printed Act of the Parliament of Great Britain from the twenty-fourth year of George II, printed at London in 1750 by Thomas Baskett, the King's Printer. The Act empowers the King to raise money by Exchequer Bills charged on the Sinking Fund, in order to pay off the Treasury's Old and New South Sea Annuities and to admit subscribers to the Bank of England and the South Sea Company. It fixes interest at four pounds per hundred a year, regulates the form, registration, and circulation of the bills, and directs the Sinking Fund to their discharge. Coming three decades after the Bubble of 1720, it marks a late stage in the long unwinding of the South Sea Company's debt, the routine statutory bookkeeping by which Britain slowly retired the obligations left by the great speculative collapse.

title: Baltimore and Ohio Railroad Company Common Stock
description: An engraved certificate for one hundred shares of common stock, par value $100 each, in the Baltimore and Ohio Railroad Company, incorporated by the State of Maryland on February 28, 1827. It was issued to Evans, Stillman & Co. and dated June 19, 1934. The B&O was among the earliest American railroads, and by the 1930s one of the great eastern trunk lines, but the 1934 date places this share in the depths of the Depression, when collapsing freight traffic and heavy fixed debt left railroad securities trading under severe strain. The engraved vignette looks back to the line's beginnings: an early upright locomotive hauls open cars past a horse-drawn stagecoach on a parallel road, a bay and sailing ships behind, setting the new railroad beside the older road transport it was built to overtake and lending the certificate a heritage of priority reaching back more than a century.

title: Baltimore and Ohio Rail Road Company Preferred Stock
description: An engraved certificate for sixty shares of the six per cent preferred stock of the Baltimore and Ohio Rail Road Company, second series, par value $100 each, issued at Baltimore and dated September 7, 1875. It rests on an act of the Maryland General Assembly of 1868, under which the company created this preferred stock and guaranteed it, by an agreement dated May 25, 1868, a perpetual dividend of six percent a year — fixed, capped at that rate, and payable ahead of any dividend to common shareholders. The certificate shows a railroad funding its post-war growth through preferred capital that stood first in line for a modest but secured return. Its vignette of a steam locomotive hauling cars across the landscape advertises the line itself, the oldest common-carrier railroad in the country, as the engine behind the investor's claim.

title: Banca Românească Share Certificate
description: A bearer share of Banca Românească, one of Romania's principal commercial banks, for a single share of 500 lei nominal value, issued at Bucharest in 1920. Because this is a bearer share, whoever held the certificate owned it, with no name registered. It dates from the years just after the First World War, when Romania was greatly enlarged by the union of Transylvania, Bessarabia, Bukovina, and the Banat, and when the bank increased its capital to 160,000,000 lei to fund commerce and production. Its allegorical vignettes tie that promise to the sources of national wealth: a standing laborer with his tool before a working harbor, a seated figure amid the fruits of the harvest, and a steamer crossing the lower border, binding labor, agriculture, and seaborne trade to the bank's prospects.

title: Banco Territorial de Cuba (Crédit Foncier Cubain), Acción Beneficiaria
description: A bearer beneficiary share of the Banco Territorial de Cuba, styled in French as the Crédit Foncier Cubain, a mortgage bank domiciled in Havana with a paid-up capital of $5,000,000 in US gold dollars. Issued at Havana on March 1, 1911 under Cuban laws of the previous year, the certificate prints its terms in four languages — Spanish, French, English, and German — signaling the European and American capital behind this land-credit institution in the young republic. It is a beneficiary share, a type of founders' share: it gave the bearer a claim on a share of the profits but, no ownership in the company's assets and no vote in its affairs. The engraved vignettes bind capital, state, and land together — a civic view of Havana, the Cuban arms and flags at the center, and a yoked ox-team hauling its load — tying the bank's fortunes to the agrarian wealth it was created to mobilize.

title: Bank Małopolski Share Certificate, Kraków
description: A joint-stock share certificate of Bank Małopolski, a Kraków bank serving the region of former Austrian Galicia, newly absorbed into the reconstituted Polish Republic. It represents twenty-five shares, dated Kraków, December 15, 1920. Each share carries a doubled denomination — 400 Austrian koron, rendered also as 280 Polish marks — a small record of the unfinished currency unification of a state stitched together from three partitioning empires, with the old Austrian crown still serving as the unit of account beside the new Polish mark. The certificate's later life is stamped across its face: subscription-right endorsements of 1922 and 1923, and an overprint revaluing the shares from 280 to 1,000 marks in 1924, as galloping inflation forced the nominal value upward.

title: Siberian Commercial Bank, Dividend Coupon Sheet
description: A sheet of five dividend coupons of the Siberian Commercial Bank, one of the leading joint-stock banks of the late Russian Empire. Each coupon entitled the holder of two shares to collect a year's dividend, running in sequence from 1917 through 1921. The coupons were printed before the revolution, for dividends reaching years into the future. But the sequence begins in 1917: after the Bolsheviks nationalized the banks that December, dividends for these years were never paid, and the sheet survives uncut and unredeemed. What was meant to be a schedule of future income became a record of income the revolution erased.

title: St. Petersburg Private Commercial Bank Share, St. Petersburg
description: A bearer share for 200 rubles in the St. Petersburg Private Commercial Bank, issued at St. Petersburg in 1911. The certificate records a joint-stock capital of 20,000,000 rubles divided into 100,000 shares, and cites the imperial confirmation of the bank's charter in 1864. Its text runs in four languages — Russian and French in the body, English and German down the borders — addressing both domestic holders and the Western European markets on which Russian banks drew, at the height of the empire's pre-war industrial boom. A sheet of dividend coupons survives attached at the left, and there the object tells a second story: the coupons run from 1914 through 1920, and those past 1917 remain uncut, dividends that went unpaid after the revolution nationalized the banks.

title: Banque Industrielle de Chine (中法實業銀行) Share, Paris
description: An ordinary bearer share, fully paid, of 500 francs in the Banque Industrielle de Chine, the Sino-French Industrial Bank, a joint-stock company seated in Paris under statutes of March 15, 1913. The certificate records a capital of 45,000,000 francs in 90,000 shares, of which 87,000 were ordinary and 3,000 founders' shares, with a marginal overprint noting a later increase of capital. The bank was established to channel French investment into Chinese commerce and industry, and the engraving advertises that purpose: dragons, a temple in the manner of Beijing's Hall of Prayer for Good Harvests, and guardian lions frame a city panorama, binding Parisian capital to its image of China. The bank suspended payments in a much-publicized failure in 1921, an event that caused heavy losses to its many French shareholders.

title: Banque Territoriale d'Espagne Share
description: A provisional bearer share of 500 francs in the Banque Territoriale d'Espagne, issued at Madrid on May 20, 1872 and here paid up to 150 francs, carrying 6 percent annual interest paid semi-annually. Constituted by acts of 1869, the bank was a land-mortgage institution modeled on France's Crédit Foncier, designed to lend against Spanish real estate and agriculture. What makes the certificate remarkable is its money: the capital of one hundred million francs is stated at once in French francs, Spanish reales, and British pounds sterling, and each share is valued in all three. That triple denomination, together with the French text on a Madrid instrument, marks a company built to straddle several markets at once, drawing on French and British investors to lend on Spanish land.

title: Compagnie Universelle du Canal Interocéanique de Panama Share
description:
A bearer share of 500 francs in the Compagnie Universelle du Canal Interocéanique de Panama, the company whose statutes were deposited before a Paris notary in October and November 1880. The certificate records a capital of 300,000,000 francs divided into 600,000 shares of 500 francs; this one is marked paid up to only 250 francs, half its value, with the balance to be called in installments. It carries the printed signature of the company's president-director, Ferdinand de Lesseps, who had triumphed a decade earlier at Suez and now raised some 1.5 billion francs from roughly 800,000 French investors to cut a canal through the Isthmus of Panama.

The venture failed catastrophically. Disease killed an estimated 22,000 workers, the sea-level design proved unbuildable, and the money ran out; in February 1889 a Paris court ordered the company liquidated, wiping out the savings of its hundreds of thousands of small subscribers. When investigators later found that the company had bribed legislators and journalists to conceal its condition, the affair became one of the defining financial and political scandals of the nineteenth century, implicating scores of members of parliament and bringing even de Lesseps and the engineer Gustave Eiffel to trial. It left the French language a new word for graft on a national scale — panamiste.

Engraved by Stern of Paris, the sheet personifies the continents as reclining figures around a globe, with border columns naming the nations. Attached coupons and installment receipts survive, the third payment recorded at Paris in February 1886.

The bond belongs to a 720-million-franc loan of two million lottery obligations authorized by the law of 8 June 1888 and offered without any guarantee of the State. title: Compagnie Universelle du Canal Maritime de Suez Obligation
description:
A bearer obligation of 500 francs, bearing 3 percent interest, issued by the Compagnie Universelle du Canal Maritime de Suez as part of a 100-million-franc loan authorized by the shareholders' assembly of June 4, 1885. Interest of 7.50 francs fell due twice a year, and the 500-franc capital was to be repaid at 575 francs through annual drawings; the attached coupons run as far as 1961, the long tail of a bond issued in the 1880s. It is signed for the board by its president, Prince Auguste d'Arenberg. The bond financed the deepening, widening, and upkeep of the Suez Canal, opened in 1869, whose revenue came from tolls on shipping crossing the Egyptian isthmus.

This is the counterpart to the Panama share in the museum. Both were bearer securities of a Compagnie Universelle led by Ferdinand de Lesseps, sold to French investors and engraved by the same Paris house, Stern — but where Suez succeeded and paid its coupons for decades, the Panama attempt collapsed in ruin. The two objects mark the triumph and the disaster of the same financier and the same model of public subscription.

The engraved frame carries a winged solar disc and globes flanking the title, with a panoramic bird's-eye view of the canal crossing the desert along the lower field.

title: Caramanian Iron Corporation Limited Share Warrant
description: A share warrant to bearer of the Caramanian Iron Corporation Limited, certifying title to ten fully paid ordinary shares of one pound each, numbered as shown, in a company capitalized at £80,000, or 2,000,000 francs. The warrant is printed in parallel English and French and gives its capital in both pounds and francs, and it was issued at Paris on February 4, 1907. Its name refers to Karamania, the region of ancient Cilicia on the southern coast of Anatolia, and the company belongs to the wave of British and French capital drawn into mineral concessions in the Ottoman Empire in its final decades. A later overprint reclassifies the instrument as a deferred share, by a resolution of an extraordinary general meeting of June 7, 1907, recording a reordering of the company's share classes only months after issue.

title: Amsterdam Depositary Certificate for Bank of the United States Shares
description:
A printed Amsterdam certificate for one share of 100 dollars in the Bank of the United States at Philadelphia. Dutch banking houses — Hope & Co., Ketwich & Voombergh, and the Widow Willem Borski — held the underlying American bank stock and issued bearer certificates like this one against it, under an administration deed of 1824, so that Dutch investors could hold and trade the shares in Amsterdam. Dividends were payable on coupons twice a year, and the attached coupons run through January 1845. It was issued at Amsterdam on January 31, 1844.

The bank named here was the Second Bank of the United States, the country's central bank and the object of one of the defining political fights in American history. President Andrew Jackson, who opposed it as a concentration of financial power, vetoed its recharter and withdrew the federal deposits; when its national charter expired in 1836 it continued as an ordinary Pennsylvania bank, which suspended payments and failed in 1841. This certificate, dated 1844, therefore represents a share in a bank that had already collapsed — a claim in its liquidation, and a record of how deeply European capital, especially Dutch, had been invested in the American central bank whose destruction Jackson had made his cause.

description: A printed Dutch-language certificate issued at Hamburg by two banking houses. It is good for an inscription of 500 roubles in the 5 percent Russian funds, payable in specie and entered in the great book of Russian government debt in the houses' name. The holder could collect interest by coupons and reclaim the underlying inscription on demand. description: A bilingual share certificate of Charles Laffitte & Company, Limited, a London finance company, for one share of £20, of which £10 was paid up. The form is printed in parallel French and English columns and dated January 15, 1866, but its fields for the holder's name and address are blank and the signature lines empty: this is an unissued blank, a printer's specimen or remainder rather than a certificate held by a shareholder. Charles Laffitte, who ran the company, was a nephew of the celebrated Paris banker and statesman Jacques Laffitte and a promoter of France's early Paris–Rouen railway. His first banking house, Charles Laffitte, Blount & Co., had failed in the revolution of 1848; this London company was the later, more modest venture he founded to rebuild.

title: Chicago, Rock Island and Pacific Railroad Company Gold Bond
description:
A registered $1,000 gold bond of the Chicago, Rock Island and Pacific Railroad Company, bearing 4 percent interest and titled the "Gold Bond of 2002." Interest was payable in gold twice a year, and both principal and interest were payable in the City of New York, with the Central Trust Company of New York as trustee. It was engraved by the American Bank Note Company.

Its striking feature is its term. The bond runs a full hundred years to its maturity on November 1, 2002 — an unusually long horizon even in railway finance, which more often issued bonds of thirty, forty, or fifty years. A century bond tied the borrower and its mortgage together across generations of investors, and the gold clause promised repayment in gold coin over that entire span. Neither promise held: the United States abandoned the gold standard in 1933, voiding such gold clauses, and the Rock Island itself did not survive to repay. After repeated reorganizations across the twentieth century, the railroad was ordered liquidated in 1980 — at the time the largest liquidation of any company in American history — twenty-two years before this bond was due to mature.

title: Republic of China Construction Gold Bonds US Dollar Bond
description:
A five-dollar bond of the Republic of China's "Construction Gold Bonds" of 1940 (the twenty-ninth year of the Republic), First US-Dollar Series, payable in United States currency. It is dated May 1, 1940 and bears the seal of the Ministry of Finance under H. H. Kung, with repayment to proceed by periodic drawing of lots. 

The bond was issued by Chiang Kai-shek's Nationalist government during the Second Sino-Japanese War, three years into a conflict in which Japan had occupied much of eastern China, including the coast and the major cities. Denominated in US dollars rather than the national currency, it was aimed at overseas Chinese communities and foreign subscribers, sources of funds the wartime government could reach when domestic revenue and borrowing fell short. H. H. Kung, its finance minister — a banker of the powerful Soong-Kung family, and brother-in-law to Chiang — had tied China's currency to the international monetary system, a policy that helped the government finance the early years of the war. Its name, the "Construction Gold Bond," and its images of dams, railways, and mines presented it as money for building up the country, but issued in the middle of the war it was in substance a war loan.

description: A 500-franc bearer bond of the Government-General of Indochina, issued under the French Republic at Paris on August 5, 1902, as part of a 200-million-franc loan authorized in 1898 to build railways in French Indochina. title: Chinese Government Loan Bond
description: A £10 bearer bond from the Chinese Government Loan of 1925, a sterling issue of £6,866,046 bearing 8 percent interest. As its text explains, it was not new money but was issued to replace and extend the unpaid portions of earlier Chinese government loans dated between 1912 and 1916, and it was sealed by the Board of Finance at Peking on September 30, 1925, under agreements with the bank formerly known as the Sino-Italian Bank. The bond was issued by the Beiyang government, the internationally recognized government of the Chinese Republic based at Peking, and it illustrates a recurring practice of the era: rather than repay foreign loans it had defaulted on, the government bundled the lapsed debts into a fresh bond at a higher rate of interest, buying relief from creditors while deepening the long-term burden. Such restructurings recurred through the 1920s, when the Republic's finances were so unstable that the finance ministry changed hands dozens of times in little more than a decade.

title: Rent Receipt (收租票) of the Zhou Household, Guangxu 22
description: A woodblock-printed rent receipt on thin fibrous paper, issued by a landlord's estate and dated the tenth month of the twenty-second year of the Guangxu reign, 1896. The form is a printed template with the particulars filled in by hand: it acknowledges rent paid in full by a named tenant farmer against a holding of land, the sum entered in copper cash and authenticated with red seals. Its printed clauses set the terms of tenancy in advance. The rent was to be paid clear by an appointed day, with no arrears allowed, failing which the land would be taken back and let to another. Printed receipts like this show how landholding estates in late Qing rural China standardized the collection of rent, fixing payment dates and the threat of eviction into a routine printed form used across many tenancies.

title: Sui Yik Loan & Godown Co. Share Certificate
description: A share certificate of the Sui Yik Loan & Godown Company, Limited, a Chinese joint-stock company, issued in 1903 (the twenty-ninth year of the Guangxu reign). The company's English name appears in its red seal, "godown" being the Asian-English word for a warehouse. As the certificate states, the firm was established for mortgage lending and warehousing, with a subscribed capital of 300,000 silver yuan divided into shares of 100 yuan each, of which 50 was paid on the first call and the balance to follow as the company required. The reverse sets out terms for transferring shares only after notice to the company. The certificate is an example of how, in the late Qing reform years, Chinese merchants adopted the Western joint-stock company, with its transferable shares and limited liability, and applied it to long-established Chinese credit practices of lending against pledged goods and storing merchants' wares.

title: 日本勧業銀行 (Hypothec Bank of Japan) Discount Debenture, 11th Issue — Sales Poster, July
description: A sales placard advertising an issue of discount debentures of the Nippon Kangyō Ginkō, the Hypothec Bank of Japan. Founded in 1897, the bank was a government-chartered "special bank" created to provide mortgage loans for agriculture and industry, and it raised money for that purpose by issuing these debentures to the public. The bonds worked as a lottery: they carried no interest coupon, but periodic drawings awarded cash prizes to lucky bond numbers, the top prize shown here as 3,000 yen. The placard advertises a short subscription window in July and sets a stylized white Mount Fuji against deep blue, in the flat color and clean lettering of modern commercial design. The lottery principle ran deep in the bank's business: in 1945 it was given the license to operate Japan's national public lottery.

title: Republic of China Third Lottery Bond (第叁次有獎公債)
description: A lottery bond of five yuan issued by the Ministry of Finance of the Nationalist Government of the Republic of China, dated August 1, 1927. Rather than pay fixed interest, bonds like this rewarded holders through periodic prize drawings, combining the appeal of a lottery with the security of a government bond to draw savings from the public. It was issued in the months after the Northern Expedition, the Nationalist military campaign that broke the power of the northern warlords and brought Chiang Kai-shek's Kuomintang government to power at Nanjing. That new government urgently needed revenue, and instruments like this one were part of how it raised money. The bond carries a portrait of Sun Yat-sen, the founder of the Chinese Republic and of the Nationalist Party, set between the crossed flags of the party and the state.

## English Translation:

**Third Lottery Bond of the Ministry of Finance, National Government** (Guómín Zhèngfǔ Cáizhèngbù Dì-sān-cì Yǒujiǎng Gōngzhài)

**Issued on the 1st day of the 8th month of the 16th year of the Republic of China** (1 August 1927)

**Five Yuan** (伍圓)

**Summary of Regulations**

1. In order to subsidize the Strike Committee (罷工委員會) and to maintain the livelihood of the workers, the National Government (Guómín Zhèngfǔ) first raised a cash loan of 5,000,000 yuan for disbursement; the Ministry of Finance therefore specially issues this Third Lottery Bond of 5,000,000 yuan to repay the said borrowing.

2. This lottery bond takes the 2.5% surcharge tax (附加二五稅) on the Guangdong (Guǎngdōng) population as its fund for repayment of principal and payment of prizes, and the Central Bank (Zhōngyāng Yínháng) bears responsibility for repayment.

3. Repayment of principal is divided into three periods, each of ten months being one period: in the first period 2% of principal is repaid each month, in the second period 3% each month, in the third period 5% each month, with the whole amount redeemed by the twentieth month; each repayment is determined by drawing lots conducted by the Ministry of Finance.

4. The interest on this bond is fixed at 50,000 yuan per month; this entire interest is allocated to prize money, and no separate interest is otherwise paid.

description: A share certificate of the Zhen-Yu Land Company, Limited, a Chinese joint-stock property company, issued in December 1944. Its share values are stated in enormous figures, counted in thousands and tens of thousands of yuan, but those numbers are a measure of collapse rather than wealth. By late 1944 Nationalist China was in the grip of extreme wartime inflation: the government had financed most of its war spending by printing money, and prices had risen to hundreds of times their prewar level, on the way to more than a thousand times by 1945. A company capitalized in the millions of yuan reflected a currency that was rapidly losing its value, not the real worth of the business.

title: Carlist Five-Percent Perpetual Rente (Ouvrard Loan), Oñate
description:
A certificate of the "Cinco Por Ciento Español," a five percent perpetual bond issued not by the government in Madrid but in the name of Don Carlos, the pretender to the Spanish throne. It was issued at Oñate, in the Basque country, on February 6, 1836, in the midst of the First Carlist War, the civil war between Don Carlos's supporters and the forces of the child queen Isabel II. The certificate promises its holder a fixed yearly payment of forty-seven pesos fuertes, in perpetuity, with the sum given also in florins, pounds, francs, and dollars, payable at Madrid or, at the holder's choice, in Amsterdam, London, Paris, Brussels, or Turin. It was contracted by Gabriel-Julien Ouvrard, one of the great speculative financiers of the Napoleonic era.

What makes the bond extraordinary is its condition: the payments were to begin only after Don Carlos entered Madrid as king. Its entire value was staked on his winning the war. He never took Madrid. The Carlists lost the war in 1839, and bonds like this were never honored, leaving them a wager on a victory that never came, issued by a claimant against the security of a throne he never reached.
creator: Government of Spain

description: A stock certificate for fifty shares, par value $100 each, in the Citrus Belt Land Company, a corporation organized under the laws of California in 1909 with a capital stock of $250,000. It was issued to S. J. White on January 26, 1911, and signed by the company's president, Geo. R. Murdock, and its secretary. The company's name places it in Southern California's "citrus belt," the region of orange groves that spread east from Pasadena through Riverside to Redlands in the decades around 1900. It belonged to the wave of land-development ventures that subdivided and sold that citrus country during the boom, when new railroads and irrigation turned dry land into groves and townsites.

title: Clădirea Românească (Romanian Building Society) Share Certificate
description: A registered share certificate of Clădirea Românească ("The Romanian Building"), a Bucharest real-estate and construction company, issued in January 1946. It conveys fifty registered shares of 500 lei each, from the company's sixth issue, against a capital of 600 million lei. The date gives it its poignancy: in January 1946 Romania was under a Soviet-backed government, but private companies still operated and raised money by selling shares like these. Within little more than two years that world was gone. In June 1948 the communist government nationalized nearly nine thousand private companies by a single law, mostly without compensation, its reach extending even to hundreds of thousands of buildings. A real-estate company like this one would have been swept away, its shares made worthless, in the final abolition of private enterprise in Romania.

title: Colombian India-Rubber Exploration Company Limited Share Warrant
description:
A bearer share warrant of The Colombian India-Rubber Exploration Company, Limited, a British-incorporated company formed to work wild-rubber concessions in Colombia. Printed in parallel English and French, it entitles the bearer to twenty-five fully paid shares of £1 each, and was issued under the company's common seal on March 4, 1907, against a capital of £300,000.

The certificate dates from the height of the Amazon rubber boom, and from a trade with a terrible history. Wild rubber in the Colombian and Peruvian Putumayo region was extracted in these years through the forced labor of Indigenous people, above all the Bora and Huitoto, under a system of debt-bondage, torture, and killing that cost tens of thousands of lives, most of it on the concessions of the British-registered Peruvian Amazon Company. This company was one of many British ventures floated to profit from Colombian rubber in exactly this period. What part it played in that trade, and whether it operated at all, is not documented here.

title: Compagnie d'Inguaran (Mexique), Part de Bénéfices
description: A bearer profit-share of the Compagnie d'Inguaran, a French company formed to work mining concessions at Inguarán, in the Mexican state of Michoacán, a district known for copper. Issued at Paris on January 15, 1898, against a capital of 3,500,000 francs, the certificate is not an ordinary share: rather than a fixed value, it entitles the bearer to a fraction of the company's profits, one part in fourteen thousand of forty percent of the net. This kind of profit-share, distinct from the voting shares, let a company's founders keep a claim on future earnings without giving up control. The company belonged to the wave of French capital drawn into Mexican mining under Porfirio Díaz, whose government actively courted foreign investment.

title: Compagnie Occidentale de Madagascar Share, Paris
description: A fully-paid 100-franc bearer share in the Compagnie Occidentale de Madagascar, a French company with its registered office in Paris, issued on September 16, 1910. The certificate records a capital of 3,200,000 francs in 32,000 shares, later raised to 7,000,000 by the overprinted stamp at its head. Its statutes date from 1895, and the company operated in Madagascar, which France had conquered and annexed as a colony in 1896. It was one of the French commercial ventures established to profit from the island after that annexation, drawing capital from investors in Paris to enterprises in a territory brought under French control by force. What the company did on the island is not detailed on the certificate, which records only its corporate structure and its Paris seat.

title: Compañía Salitrera de Tarapacá y Antofagasta share certificate, Santiago
description:
A bearer certificate for ten shares of fifty pesos each, fully paid, in the Compañía Salitrera de Tarapacá y Antofagasta, known as COSATAN, a Chilean nitrate company. It was issued at Santiago on April 30, 1937, and the company had been formed in 1934, by the supreme decree named on the certificate, from the merger of thirty-four nitrate producers.

COSATAN was created out of a catastrophe. Chile's northern deserts had long supplied much of the world's nitrate, used for fertilizer and explosives, an industry that once accounted for around half of the country's income. Then synthetic nitrogen, first produced in Germany early in the century, undercut it: cheap manufactured fertilizer drove prices down while mining costs rose, and the desert industry collapsed. COSATAN was assembled in 1934 from the wreckage, but it inherited heavy debt and by 1960 had itself gone bankrupt. This share, issued in 1937, is a document of that long decline, an investment in an industry a laboratory process had already doomed.

title: Companhia de Mossamedes Share Warrant to Bearer for Five Shares
description:
A trilingual bearer share warrant of the Companhia de Mossamedes, a Portuguese colonial company, for five fully-paid shares of 4.50 escudos each. Printed in Portuguese, French, and English and issued to circulate among European investors, it drew capital toward a venture at Moçâmedes (now Namibe), a port in southern Angola, then ruled by Portugal as part of its African empire. The capital and share terms on its face were fixed by company assemblies between 1901 and 1928.

The certificate belongs to the era of Portuguese colonial enterprise in Angola, when companies raised money in Europe to profit from territories Portugal governed and their populations. Portuguese colonial economies of this period rested heavily on African labor that was often forced or coerced. What this particular company did in Angola is not recorded on the certificate, which shows only its capital structure and its shares.

title: Madrid-Zaragoza-Alicante Railway Company Share
description: An engraved bearer share in the Compañía de los Ferro-Carriles de Madrid a Zaragoza y a Alicante, the MZA, one of Spain's two principal railway companies. Printed in parallel Spanish and French, it certifies one share of 1,900 reales, equal to 500 francs, and was dated at Madrid on July 1, 1859. The company's capital of 456 million reales, or 120 million francs, was divided into 240,000 shares. The MZA was founded in 1856 with French money, controlled by the Paris house of Rothschild, and its great rival, the Norte company, was backed by the competing French bank of the Pereire brothers. The share's dual denomination in reales and francs, and its bilingual text, reflect that French capital, which built much of Spain's railway network after the country opened to foreign railway investment under a law of 1855.

description: A $500 coupon bond of the Confederate States of America, issued under a loan authorized by act of the Confederate Congress on August 19, 1861. # Council of the Apportioned Public Debt of the Former Ottoman Empire — Bearer Provisional Receipt for the 5% Ottoman Loan of 1914 — Transcription

## Original:

(Ornamental engraved border framing the whole certificate; the outer top border repeats "…PUBLIQUE RÉPARTIE DE L'ANCIEN EMPIRE OTTOMAN".)

**CONSEIL DE LA DETTE PUBLIQUE RÉPARTIE DE L'ANCIEN EMPIRE OTTOMAN**

**RÉCÉPISSÉ PROVISOIRE AU PORTEUR N° 0,288,837**

délivré contre retrait d'une obligation unitaire d'un capital nominal de Frs. 500 ou £ 19,17 ou Ltqs. 22

**DE L'EMPRUNT OTTOMAN 5 % 1914.**

Conformément à la décision en date du 9 Juin 1933 de la Commission pour la répartition du capital nominal de la Dette Publique Ottomane, instituée par l'Article 49 du Traité de Lausanne, le présent récépissé a été délivré, contre retrait de l'obligation susvisée, par l'entremise de la Banque
pour constater :

*a)* que la quote-part de la Turquie a fait l'objet d'une émission spéciale ; que les quotes-parts de l'Italie (Dodécanèse), de la Palestine, de l'Irak et des États du Levant sous Mandat français ont été entièrement amorties ;

*b)* et que, par suite de ces règlements, à la date d'émission du présent récépissé, le capital nominal non amorti de l'emprunt susvisé se trouve réduit aux montants indiqués dans le tableau ci-dessous, incombant aux États qui en sont les débiteurs à raison des montants énoncés en regard de chacun d'eux.

(Table. Column headers, left to right: **ÉTATS DÉBITEURS** | **Proportions %** | **Capital non amorti sur les 804,675 titres unitaires de l'emprunt susvisé restant en circulation à la date d'émission du présent récépissé** [sub-columns: **Frs.** | **ou £** | **ou Ltqs.**] | **Capital non amorti de chaque titre unitaire de l'emprunt susvisé** [sub-columns: **Frs.** | **ou £** | **ou Ltqs.**])

| ÉTATS DÉBITEURS | Prop. % | Frs. | ou £ | ou Ltqs. | Frs. | ou £ | ou Ltqs. |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| GRÈCE | 13,31 | 2.639.364 | 104.783 | 116.132 | 3,28 | 0,13 | 0,14 |
| BULGARIE | 3,83 | 760.636 | 30.197 | 33.468 | 0,95 | 0,04 | 0,04 |
| TRANSJORDANIE (y compris le Caza de Maan) | 19,32 | 3.831.023 | 152.092 | 168.565 | 4,76 | 0,19 | 0,21 |
| HEDJAZ | 33,59 | 6.661.727 | 264.470 | 293.116 | 8,28 | 0,33 | 0,36 |
| ASSYR | 0,58 | 116.114 | 4.610 | 5.109 | 0,14 | 0,01 | 0,01 |
| YEMEN | 26,48 | 5.251.568 | 208.487 | 231.069 | 6,53 | 0,26 | 0,29 |
| NEDJD | 2,89 | 573.773 | 22.779 | 25.246 | 0,71 | 0,02 | 0,03 |
| **TOTAL** | **100, »** | **19.834.205** | **787.418** | **872.705** | **24,65** | **0,98** | **1,08** |

Le présent récépissé provisoire est exclusivement émis pour constater les droits des porteurs des titres retirés de la circulation sur les États débiteurs indiqués ci-dessus. Ces États ne pourront procéder, par le rachat de ces récépissés, à l'amortissement du capital nominal à leur charge dans la Dette Ottomane. Le Conseil de la Dette, détenteur des titres ottomans retirés de la circulation, aura seul qualité pour procéder aux paiements ou autres opérations qui pourront être effectués au moyen du présent récépissé provisoire, en vue de l'application des Accords conclus avec les États pour le règlement de leurs quotes-parts dans la Dette Ottomane. Les coupons nos 1 à 12 attachés au présent récépissé serviront à constater les dits paiements ou opérations, dont les modalités seront portées, en temps utile, à la connaissance des porteurs, par des avis publiés par le Conseil de la Dette.

**POUR CONTRÔLE,**
*Par Délégation du Conseil :*
[handwritten signature — illegible]

**POUR LE CONSEIL DE LA DETTE PUBLIQUE RÉPARTIE DE L'ANCIEN EMPIRE OTTOMAN,**
*Le Président :*
[handwritten signature — illegible]

Paris, le 1er Octobre 1933.

title: Dutch Coupons for American Land Shares, C.J.M. De Wolf, Antwerp

notes: Two Dutch coupons No. 827, 50 Gulden each for f.1000 American land shares, payable at C.J.M. De Wolf, Antwerp, June 1795 and June 1796

title: The Cuba Company Common Stock Certificate
description: A specimen common stock certificate of The Cuba Company, incorporated in New Jersey, with the share value and holder details left blank. It is marked "SPECIMEN" in red, and the date and signature lines are empty. The certificate names Central Union Trust Company of New York as registrar and The National City Bank of New York as transfer agent. The registrar operated under that name only between 1918 and 1929, dating the specimen to that period.

notes: The Cuba Company, common stock specimen certificate, State of New Jersey; company built the Cuba Railroad ca. 1900

title: Ostend Company (Generale Keijserlijcke Indische Compagnie) Share Subscription Receipt

title: Grand Society of Russian Railways (Главное Общество Российских Железных Дорог) Silver Bond
description: A 3 percent bearer bond of 125 silver rubles issued by the Grand Society of Russian Railways, based in St. Petersburg, from its third issue. The bond's value is given in several currencies alongside the ruble: 500 francs, 20 pounds sterling, 402 German marks, and 236 Dutch guilders. It paid interest twice a year, and it is dated at St. Petersburg, December 23, 1880, by the old Russian calendar, corresponding to January 4, 1881. Paying agents are listed in Paris, Berlin, London, and Brussels.
creator: Grand Society of Russian Railways (Главное Общество Российских Железных Дорог)
notes: Grand Society of Russian Railways, Third Issue, 125 Ruble Silver Bond No. 220757, 3%, = 500 Francs = £20 = 402 German Marks = 238 Dutch Gulden

Основной капиталъ Общества по Уставу ВЫСОЧАЙШЕ утвержденному 3-го Ноября 1861 г.:

въ акціяхъ: 600,000 акцій по 125 рублей сер. на 75,000,000 руб. сер. (металл.)

Выкупъ, по нарицательной цѣнѣ, производится посредствомъ ежегоднаго тиража по жеребью, въ теченіе 70 лѣтъ, ¹⁄₁₃ Іюня каждаго года, начиная съ ¹⁄₁₃ Іюня 1881 года. Выдача суммъ погашенія по облигаціямъ, вышедшимъ въ тиражъ производится ¹⁄₁₃ Декабря каждаго года, начиная съ ¹⁄₁₃ Декабря 1881 года.

**№220757**

(Seal at right margin: **М.Ф. 1**)

(Top left:) **125 rubles**  (Top right:) **3%**

**GRAND SOCIETY OF RUSSIAN RAILWAYS,**

established by IMPERIAL Decree of 26 January 1857.

SEAT OF THE SOCIETY AT ST. PETERSBURG.

Founding capital of the Society under the Charter IMPERIALLY approved 3 November 1861:

in shares: 600,000 shares of 125 silver rubles = 75,000,000 silver rubles (metallic);

title: Italian Public Debt Rendita Certificate
description: A certificate of the Public Debt of the Kingdom of Italy, bearing five percent interest under the law of July 10, 1861, inscribed in the Grand Book of the Public Debt. It records a perpetual annuity of 20 lire a year, payable in two installments on January 1 and July 1. The annuity was registered in favor of the parish church of San Rocco, near Udine, administered by its own board of works. The certificate was issued at Florence on August 5, 1874, and carries a portrait of King Victor Emmanuel II. It is stamped "annullato," cancelled.
creator: Kingdom of Italy, Ministry of Finance
notes: Debito Pubblico del Regno d'Italia, 5% Rendita, annual income 20 lire, issued from Florence; portrait of Victor Emmanuel II

title: Deli Railway Company Share
description: A share certificate for one share of 1,000 guilders in the Deli-Spoorweg-Maatschappij (Deli Railway Company), a limited company based at Amsterdam with a capital of 10,000,000 guilders. The company was founded in 1883, and this share was issued at Amsterdam on May 5, 1914, signed by the president-commissioner and a director. Its name refers to the Deli district of East Sumatra, in the Netherlands East Indies, where the company operated a railway. It was printed by Joh. Enschedé en Zonen of Haarlem.
